name: Alabama
region: Southeast / Alabama River; Louisiana migration; Texas and Oklahoma communities
overview: Explore Alabama history, language and continuing community life through annotated sources. This introduction follows southeastern connections, Texas and Oklahoma settings, original government documents and community language work, with remaining gaps kept visible.

sections.title: A people and language, with several community settings
sections.text: Alabama is a people and language name, distinct from the modern state’s broader Indigenous population. Closely related Coushatta/Quassarte communities share parts of this history. The reading below follows Texas and Oklahoma settings separately.

sections.title: Southeastern towns and different westward journeys
sections.text: John H. Moore’s historical reference follows Alabama and Quassarte towns along the Alabama River into French trade relationships and the Creek Confederacy. It describes westward movement in separate groups, including settlements in central Louisiana and Texas, while people who remained with the Creeks underwent forced removal to Indian Territory. These were different community histories, rather than one journey followed by everyone.

sections.title: A Texas community's account of its past
sections.text: The Tribe's public history places Alabama and Coushatta origins in neighboring areas of what is now Alabama, followed by westward movement into Texas. It connects the Texas community's history with alliances, assistance to refugees during the 1836 conflict and the restoration of federal recognition in 1987. This is the Tribe's concise account of its past. Its references to promised or recognized lands should be read alongside the underlying agreements, rather than converted into a present property map.

sections.title: Villages, rivers and paths in East Texas
sections.text: Howard Martin’s Handbook history describes Alabama settlements along waterways including the Angelina and Neches rivers. Peach Tree, Fenced-In and Cane Island appear as distinct villages connected through trails. The account links hunting, cultivation and travel to the Big Thicket landscape, then follows settler pressure and land disputes. Read its route descriptions as a historian’s reconstruction, with particular family movements still requiring closer archival comparison.

sections.title: Different leaders and a shared reservation
sections.text: Chief History separately presents leaders of Alabama villages, Coushatta villages and the later Alabama-Coushatta community. That structure preserves distinctions within a connected history. Its biographies describe Colabe's multilingual interpreting and John Scott's role as a school trustee, linking leadership with diplomacy and education. The introductory settlement account explains how sharing the Polk County reservation encouraged the joint Texas name. It should not be stretched into a claim that all Alabama or Coushatta people everywhere became one government.

sections.title: What the 1954 termination act changed
sections.text: The 1954 federal act authorized conveyance of tribal land to Texas to hold in trust. It tied termination of the federal trust relationship to conveyance and a subsequent proclamation, and withdrew status-based federal Indian services while retaining specified school and hospital eligibility. This legislation changed federal administration and obligations. The enactment and its later implementation should be distinguished: the proclamation has not been inspected for this introduction.

sections.title: Restoring the federal relationship in 1987
sections.text: Title II of the act approved August 18, 1987 restored federal recognition and the trust relationship for the Alabama and Coushatta Indian Tribes of Texas. It treated the two as one tribal unit for federal-law purposes and addressed the council’s powers, constitution and reservation. The act’s separate title for Ysleta del Sur Pueblo should not be applied to Alabama-Coushatta. This primary document explains an important historical change; later legal developments need their own sources.

sections.title: Constitutional government and cultural responsibilities
sections.text: The July 2023 constitutional consolidation records an original adoption in 1971 and later amendments. It names the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas as the joint legal and governmental unit, then distinguishes chiefs, a seven-member council, administration and courts. Chiefs have cultural, historical and advisory responsibilities; council members serve staggered three-year terms under that text. Its preamble connects self-government with education, language, arts and cultural preservation. These provisions belong to the Texas government's constitutional history.

sections.title: Reading the Oklahoma community's own history
sections.text: An undated community account distinguishes Alabama and Quassarte towns while describing their Muscogee relationships. It presents southwestern migration and removal to Indian Territory as different historical paths, and describes traditional government continuing through federal changes. Read this as a particular Oklahoma community's interpretation, alongside primary records. Its account does not make the Oklahoma and Texas governments interchangeable; claims about present membership or administration require separately dated evidence.

sections.title: A historical constitution and its two dates
sections.text: The 1939 government printing identifies Alabama and Quassarte No. 1 as former towns within Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town. Its purposes include land, economic cooperation, health, welfare and continuing traditions. The Interior approval block is dated November 17, 1938; certification separately records ratification on January 10, 1939. Article IX protects existing rights as citizens of the Creek Nation. These are historical provisions, not an independent statement of present citizenship, leadership or governing law.

sections.title: Education, language and women's leadership
sections.text: The Tribal Council's 2023 tribute describes Millie Ann Thompson Williams as the first woman elected to a chief position for the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe. It connects her leadership with many years of Head Start teaching and identifies her as an Alabama-language teacher and preservation consultant. This public remembrance makes a named educator's contribution visible alongside formal government history. Her biography connects community education with formal political leadership.

sections.title: Alabama and Koasati are related languages
sections.text: Alabama belongs to the Muskogean family and is closely related to Koasati, also called Coushatta. Their relationship should be kept distinct from the shared name of the Texas tribal government. A resource for one language is not automatically a description of the other.

sections.title: A dictionary built into a learning collection
sections.text: Cora Sylestine’s educator-led dictionary work underlies a continuing learning collection. The 1993 preface credits her initiative and later collaboration with Heather K. Hardy and Timothy Montler. The current Alabama Dictionary Online adds grammatical explanations and teaching materials through a Texas tribal–WOLF Lab partnership. Its June 2025 verb handout moves from introductions to changing verb forms and partner exercises; the noun guide explains how endings mark a noun’s role. The project says speakers approve public recordings and collected material is owned by and shared with the tribe. The lessons make vocabulary and grammatical relationships accessible through a community collaboration.

sections.title: Community experience within language research
sections.text: In a 2024 interview, Ava Silva connects Alabama learning with listening to her grandmother and with the older generation’s painful experiences of punishment at school. Rojas’s article identifies Silva as the project’s community coordinator and a participant in research on verb conjugations. It also describes recordings shared with the community and findings presented to the tribal council. This attributed account helps readers understand the family and community relationships within documentation, while Silva’s experience should not be generalized to every Alabama family.

sections.title: Questions being investigated in Alabama grammar
sections.text: Fernandes and Silva’s January 2026 conference presentation examines how Alabama changes verbs to identify participants in an action. They compare earlier placement rules with additional examples and propose that different stages of word formation help explain why agreement markers appear in different positions. Worked derivations and an unresolved question about negation make the talk a substantial research resource. Readers should distinguish the authors’ proposed analysis from established consensus; the presentation offers neither a complete grammar nor a guide to every speaker’s usage.

sections.title: Making time and materials for learning
sections.text: Harvard’s September 2026 report describes three June community workshops, including pronunciation, greetings, possession and verb grammar. It also reports weekly online instruction and tribal approval of one paid hour a week for employees to attend. These are concrete, dated actions supporting access to learning. The report does not measure proficiency gains or establish that everyone participates; its value lies in documenting how a particular collaboration was being organized in 2026.

sections.title: Planning for everyday access
sections.text: The Tribe's April 2025 transportation plan connects infrastructure with the daily needs of residents and visitors. It describes drainage and road-surface problems, coordinating health, education, emergency and transportation departments with external partners. Its strategies include further investigation, seeking funds and developing longer-lasting maintenance solutions. This is a practical example of government planning for community life. The published final draft records goals and a schedule; it does not independently establish that every project was adopted, funded or completed.

name: Aleut (Unangax̂)
region: Alaska / Aleutian Islands, western Alaska Peninsula and Pribilof communities
overview: Unangax̂ histories connect the Aleutian Islands and western Alaska Peninsula with the Pribilofs, urban Alaska and wider family networks. This reading collection brings community publications into conversation with university resources, survivor recollections, an official wartime investigation and original restitution legislation. It distinguishes regional institutions from individual tribal governments and historical evidence from current conditions.

sections.title: Names, dialects and distinct neighboring peoples
sections.text: Unangam Tunuu is the language name. The university introduction distinguishes Eastern and Western dialects and explains Unangan and Unangas as plural forms, alongside singular Unangax̂. Older Russian use of Aleut covered more than one Alaska Native people. Unangax̂ and Alutiiq/Sugpiaq should therefore remain distinct directory entries; a shared colonial label does not make their languages or governments interchangeable.

sections.title: Homelands, colonial movement and distinct institutions
sections.text: APIA’s historical synthesis places Unangax̂ homelands across the Aleutian chain, Shumagin Islands and western Alaska Peninsula. It describes Russian fur-trade coercion and the compelled movement of Aleutian villagers to the Pribilof Islands, where year-round settlements developed by the early nineteenth century. These colonial movements form part of community history rather than a single unchanging settlement pattern. The account also distinguishes the Aleut Corporation, a shareholder-owned regional business, from APIA, a nonprofit providing tribal services. Neither institution should be substituted for the governments of individual communities.

sections.title: Maritime knowledge and material life
sections.text: The NPS introduction describes ulax̂ houses built partly into the ground and seasonal camps supporting harvesting. Skin-covered iqyax̂ kayaks joined carefully fitted frames with waterproof sewing. Animal materials supplied food, clothing, tools and containers; grass weaving produced baskets. These are historical technologies requiring skill and environmental knowledge. The contemporary teaching accounts below help connect this material history with continuing cultural learning.

sections.title: One community’s constitutional framework
sections.text: The Qawalangin constitution speaks for a particular Unangan government connected with Unalaska, Sedanka and Amaknak islands. Its preamble links self-government with collective cultural, social and economic wellbeing. The posted document provides for a seven-member elected council and protects civil rights, including a qualified right for members to review tribal records. Its certification records an adoption election on May 3, 1997. This is evidence of this government’s constitutional framework at adoption; it does not establish that all Unangax̂ communities share one constitution or that no amendments followed.

sections.title: Environmental oversight in Unalaska
sections.text: Qawalangin’s environmental program makes another part of self-government visible: maintaining an inventory, reviewing technical documents, seeking community input and coordinating assessment or cleanup. Its linked public record distinguishes proposed investigation from completed actions and identifies work that remains incomplete. These distinctions matter when learning about the continuing responsibilities created by contamination. The record supports an account of oversight and ongoing work; it is not a general assurance that a listed place is safe or unrestricted.

sections.title: St. Paul priorities in a changing marine economy
sections.text: In its February 2023 newsletter, the Aleut Community of St. Paul Island connects economic resilience with the health of the surrounding sea. Leadership describes the crab-fishery crisis and efforts to diversify the island economy. Conservation staff report community engagement around the PRIME initiative and work on Indigenous monitoring, including attention to data sovereignty and intellectual-property rights. These are dated accounts of priorities and work underway, not confirmation that every proposed project was completed. The sanctuary nomination discussed there should not be described as an established marine sanctuary.

sections.title: An urban gathering for cultural learning
sections.text: APIA describes its Anchorage culture camp as a gathering connecting participants from the islands, urban Alaska and farther afield. Learning involves different ages: Elders share memories and family connections, children rotate through activities, and older participants choose areas of interest. Activities offered over the years include sewing, basketry and boat-building. The page presents cultural learning as something communities continue to shape in an urban setting. Its historical list of activities should not be read as the schedule for any particular year.

sections.title: Literacy as collaborative work
sections.text: The university traces writing and teaching materials through work involving Unangax̂ speakers, including William Dirks Sr. and Moses Dirks, alongside linguists. Its CoLang 2016 examples describe reuse of earlier learning materials. This introduction is a route into that history; the linked dictionaries, grammars and digital tools have not all been reviewed here.

sections.title: Teacher preparation and community direction
sections.text: APIA describes lesson creation, learning from speakers, intensives and oral proficiency assessment. Its 2019 grant sought a regional teacher-certification pilot; a target of additional teachers is not a measured outcome. Elders, speakers and community members selected through tribal councils advise regional language work. The page also describes Eastern and Atka classes, but its undated timetable is not presented here as a verified current schedule.

sections.title: U.S. removal and survival in Southeast Alaska
sections.text: After the 1942 attacks, U.S. authorities removed villagers to Southeast Alaska. The NPS account documents makeshift camp buildings, unsafe water, inadequate care and deadly illness. It also describes evacuees finding work, repairing housing and establishing community facilities. These actions belong in the account alongside government neglect: displaced families continued organizing daily life under conditions they had not chosen.

sections.title: Wartime decisions and federal responsibility
sections.text: The 1982 commission distinguished the Aleut evacuation from Japanese American exclusion: it considered removal from islands under attack a reasonable safety precaution. It nevertheless documented failures to plan, deplorable camps, looted homes and delayed return. Keeping those findings together explains how an evacuation prompted by a real attack became a history of preventable official harm.

sections.title: Attu captivity and the limits of return
sections.text: Attu residents faced a separate ordeal: Japanese forces took them to Japan. In Attu Boy, Nick Golodoff recalls confinement, hunger and illness through a child's memories; his granddaughter and editor make their uncertainties visible. His return account describes being sent to Atka, where relatives provided housing. Survival and release therefore did not mean restoration of his former home on Attu.

sections.title: Survivors' advocacy and redress
sections.text: Survivors and community members pressed for recognition by recounting traumatic experiences, documenting losses and taking their case to Washington. The NPS restitution account presents this as sustained Unangax̂ organizing. Its survivor perspectives also show why acknowledgment and funds could assist rebuilding without replacing lost relatives, homes or cultural belongings.

sections.title: What the 1988 enactment addressed
sections.text: Public Law 100–383 acknowledged U.S. failures of care and property protection. Title II separated community losses from individual compensation for defined eligible persons. It addressed Attu land losses principally through compensation while also authorizing limited site conveyances. These historical provisions do not establish that every authorized action occurred or that Attu village was restored.

sections.title: Using archives with their limits in view
sections.text: The university archive guide identifies linguistic and educational collections, including materials concerning the Commander Islands. Its finding aid can guide further investigation, but a collection description is not inspection of every item. Reproduction and use restrictions apply to some material; linked records and recordings need their own contextual review.

A directory and archival finding aid remain outside the substantive target. Coverage is broad enough to continue alphabetically, while the gaps below remain open.

name: Alsea
overview: Alsea histories connect the central Oregon coast with families and the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians. This collection follows river-valley names, dispossession, political continuity, an Alsea photographer and historical language documentation. It distinguishes Alsea people from the multi-people federal subagency and places confederated accounts and neighboring witnesses in their stated contexts.

sections.title: People, river valleys and place names
sections.text: The educational place-name account describes Alsea and Yaquina as central-coast peoples and connects their names with river valleys. Ya’xaik is the Alsea village name behind the later English Yachats. A village, a river valley, a language variety, the present town and the later federal subagency are different subjects. Keeping them distinct makes the historical record easier to follow without turning all reservation residents into one people.

sections.title: Alsea continuity within a confederated community
sections.text: The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians includes Alsea among its ancestral peoples while emphasizing that each has a distinct history, culture and legal relationship. The Tribe also explains that many members identify their ancestry through particular villages or bands. Alsea continuity within Siletz therefore need not erase those more specific family connections, nor imply that the many ancestral peoples became culturally interchangeable.

sections.title: A people and an administrative institution
sections.text: The Alsea Subagency was a federal administrative institution, rather than another name for all Alsea people. David Lewis describes its officials managing Alsea, Siuslaw, Lower Umpqua, Coos and Coquille communities. Its later closure therefore affected several distinct peoples. His account also follows people who moved to Siletz and others who remained in off-reservation homelands; closure of the institution did not mean disappearance of its former residents or their descendants.

sections.title: Resource pressure and loss of reservation land
sections.text: Lewis's oyster-rush study places reservation reduction within a struggle over resources. Miners, harvesters and squatters sought access to Yaquina Bay while federal agents attempted to exclude unauthorized settlers. Commercial demand for oysters linked the bay to San Francisco markets. This account connects land opening with economic and political pressure, rather than portraying removal as an isolated administrative adjustment. Its setting encompasses several coastal peoples, including Alsea and Yaquina communities.

sections.title: Remembering occupied homelands and objections to removal
sections.text: The Tribe’s account of reservation reduction disputes the official claim that coastal land was unoccupied or unwanted. It specifically describes Alsea and Yaquina villages still occupied by their people during the 1860s. Its later article recounts Yachats residents’ resistance to another removal. Read alongside the federal records, this perspective keeps residents’ presence and objections visible when administrative documents describe land being opened to settlers.

sections.title: How consolidation was argued in Congress
sections.text: The February 1875 Senate debate presents a proposal to remove people from Alsea and Siletz reservation lands into a smaller designated area and open the remainder to settlement. Senator Mitchell justified consolidation partly by eliminating the expense of a second agent. Other senators questioned procedure and funding. This is evidence of how officials argued for the measure; it neither establishes community agreement nor substitutes for checking the subsequently enacted law.

sections.title: Reading testimony from the shared reservation system
sections.text: In Lewis's abridged presentation of 1931 claims testimony, Annie Peterson identifies herself as Coos and recalls hardship at Yahaats and assistance from Siuslaw people afterward. Other witnesses describe work, inadequate provisions and movement between communities. These accounts help readers understand the wider Alsea reservation system. Their named community affiliations and differing firsthand knowledge should remain visible; they cannot be silently converted into testimony about every Alsea family's experience.

sections.title: An Alsea photographer and the power of representation
sections.text: Siletz’s photography lesson identifies Thomas C. Jackson as Alsea, with family from near present-day Waldport. It follows his return to Siletz after studying photography and his work making portraits, community scenes and landscapes. The lesson asks readers to consider how Native people represented themselves and their families, rather than treating every historical photograph as an outsider’s record of disappearance. Jackson’s photographs offer a concrete Alsea connection to that history.

sections.title: Termination, organizing and restoration
sections.text: The Tribe’s restoration lesson distinguishes the 1954 termination law from its implementation in 1956. Its account describes the loss of services and land alongside Siletz families’ grassroots organizing to regain federal recognition in 1977. This is a confederated political history relevant to Alsea descendants within Siletz. A change in federal recognition should not be read as the disappearance and later recreation of the people themselves.

sections.title: A participant in the restoration movement
sections.text: Addressing the Senate in 1976, Siletz council member Pauline Bell Ricks described rebuilding the council through elections, meetings and community participation. She explained that people who had moved away for work still understood Siletz as home and returned for gatherings and the restoration campaign. Her testimony adds a participant’s account of continued relationships during termination. It speaks to the confederated community; it should not be recast as testimony from a separately identified Alsea government.

sections.title: Contemporary priorities for coastal land return
sections.text: An October 2026 report records Siletz officials discussing a proposed coastal land return near Yachats. Council member Alfred Lane IV connects the place with memories of people confined at the Alsea Subagency, while natural resources director Angela Sondenaa discusses renewed stewardship and gathering opportunities. The article describes the transfer as still underway, so it supports a dated account of community priorities and expectations, rather than confirmation of completed ownership or a separate Alsea-only landholding.

sections.title: Named speakers and the making of a historical record
sections.text: Frachtenberg’s introduction names William Smith and Thomas Jackson among the Alsea contributors to his work and identifies earlier material collected by Livingston Farrand. He explains revising transcription and arranging translated texts. The vocabulary introduction also describes combining records from different investigators. These editorial choices shaped the published record; its limitations and colonial judgments should remain visible rather than being treated as a complete inventory of Alsea knowledge.

sections.title: What the noun-phrase study reveals
sections.text: Buckley examines how Alsea noun phrases identify a referent, express possession and mark relationships such as movement toward a place. His study follows small grammatical elements whose placement depends on phrase structure, including a marker that appears after different words as the phrase changes. He also identifies questions the available texts cannot settle. These patterns and proposed explanations offer a focused introduction to grammar, rather than a complete teaching course or a present-day language-use survey.

sections.title: How an event unfolds in recorded Alsea
sections.text: Buckley’s study asks how Alsea verbs present an event’s beginning, end or resulting state. He argues that suffixes do more than correspond to English past-tense translations: context can make the same form appear differently in English. His comparison of earlier transcriptions and translations shows why wording in a translated text may conceal a grammatical distinction. This is a proposed analysis of recorded language, rather than evidence about present speakers or the continuity of Alsea families.

sections.title: Archives preserve distinct languages and research histories
sections.text: The Smithsonian finding aid identifies Alsea texts and notes alongside a separate Lower Umpqua grammatical index. It also records corrected notebook authorship. Shared storage does not establish that these are the same language. Likewise, the state teaching account identifies Siletz Dee-ni as a Dené language; the confederation’s name does not make all its language resources Alsea lessons.

sources.title: Selected English Place Names with Indigenous Origins in Western Oregon
sources.publisher: Oregon Department of Education; Tribal History/Shared History
sources.annotation: Educational account connects Alsea and Yaquina names with river valleys and distinguishes Ya’xaik from later English spellings. Its neighboring-language sections help prevent conflation. Use the stated historical scope, rather than treating modern administrative regions as Indigenous boundaries.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual PDF pages 1–2 read, plus Dee-ni language introduction on pages 3–4. No full nine-page review or inspection of its cited works claimed. Sensitive burial detail omitted from synthesis.

sources.title: Our Heritage history series: Introduction and the reservation reductions
sources.annotation: The Tribe’s substantive history identifies Alsea within the confederation and challenges official accounts of empty land and consent. Three related articles form one unit; general regional practices are not assigned uniformly to Alsea.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read Introduction, lines 128–139; the substantive 1865 article, lines 128–153; and the 1875 article, lines 128–155. Individual authorship and original publication dates are not stated on these pages.

inspectedSubresources.title: Changing Federal Policy & Reduction of the Coast Reservation by Act of Congress, 1875

sources.title: Alsea Subagency of Siletz Reservation
sources.author: David G. Lewis
sources.annotation: Substantive account of the multi-people subagency, land reductions, removal and descendant communities. Its administrative labels must be separated from Alsea identity. Use the 1865 executive-order chronology rather than repeating the article's congressional attribution.
sources.contentReviewScope: Entire main historical narrative, bibliography and update metadata; article paragraphs beginning September 1856 through descendants. 1865 congressional attribution is inaccurate; distinguish the December 21 executive order from 1875 legislation. Descendant governments listed concern all subagency peoples, not every Alsea family.

sources.title: Opening the Coast Reservation: the Oyster Harvest Rush 1863–1866
sources.publisher: The Quartux Journal / Critical Indigenous Perspectives
sources.author: David G. Lewis
sources.annotation: Connects settler intrusion at Yaquina with mining rumors, commercial oyster harvesting and pressure to open reservation land. Useful for the economic setting of Alsea-area displacement, with the broader multi-people Coast Reservation scope retained.
sources.contentReviewScope: Main authored essay, especially Huntington's responses, oyster trade, and Reduction of Coast reservation in 1865 paragraphs. Embedded archival images not independently transcribed/read. Acreage, jurisdictional conclusions, unrelated peoples' losses and the essay's Congress-in-1865 wording not adopted.

sources.title: Congressional Record, February 20, 1875: Alsea and Siletz reservation amendment debate
sources.author: United States Senate; remarks and proposal by Senator John H. Mitchell, with other senators
sources.annotation: Selected Senate debate exposes the proposal's removal and settlement-opening language and Mitchell's cost-saving rationale. It records legislative argument and procedural decisions, not affected communities' consent or an independently inspected final enactment.
sources.contentReviewScope: Printed pp. 1528–1529 (PDF pages 9–10): Mitchell proposal/rationale, funding debate and procedural disposition. OCR columns interleave; keep procedural claims narrow. The committee-stage amendment's adoption does not establish final statutory language or implementation.

sources.title: Oral Histories of Native Experiences at Yahaats Sub-Agency
sources.publisher: The Quartux Journal / Critical Indigenous Perspectives
sources.author: David G. Lewis; named witnesses in an abridged 1931 Coos claims transcript
sources.annotation: Lewis presents abridged Coos claims testimony about Yahaats within the Alsea reservation system. Witnesses distinguish their experiences, movements and knowledge. This is direct shared-institutional history, not Alsea-authored testimony or a statement of Alsea cultural practices. Inspected contextual reading, outside the Alsea substantive target.
sources.scopeClassification: Shared reservation-system context; witnesses largely concern Coos communities
sources.contentReviewScope: Introductory scope/abridgment explanation and printed testimony excerpts, especially George W. Jackson, James Buchanan, Frank Drew and Annie Peterson. Original 1931 court transcript not independently read. No aggregate death rate, compensation chronology or broad legal conclusion adopted. Reader comments excluded.

sources.title: Tribal History/Shared History: selected photography, termination and restoration lessons
sources.annotation: Actual tribal lesson PDFs provide Alsea-specific Jackson history and wider confederated political context. Count the collection once. Their treatment of photographs does not establish image-reproduction permission.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read photography lesson pages 1–5, termination pages 1–4 and restoration pages 1–4. Visually checked photography pages 3–4 and restoration page 3; other selected pages were read as PDF text.
sources.publicationDate: Undated lesson texts; URLs filed in December 2023

inspectedSubresources.title: Whose Lens? Photography and Representation — Grade 11
inspectedSubresources.scope: Selected pages 1–5 of 18; synthesis uses pages 3–4.

inspectedSubresources.title: The Restoration Movement, 1956–1977 — Grade 10
inspectedSubresources.scope: Selected pages 1–4 of 16; 1954/1956 distinction on page 1, restoration account on page 3.

sources.title: Siletz Restoration Act hearings: selected tribal testimony, March 30–31, 1976
sources.publisher: United States Senate; tribal testimony republished for the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians curriculum
sources.annotation: Pauline Bell Ricks supplies an Indigenous first-person account within a federal hearing. This is confederated testimony, not proof of her Alsea ancestry, unanimity or a separate Alsea government. The teaching extract omits intervening pages.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read cover and PDF pages 2–5, corresponding to printed pages 39, 42–43 and 45; visually checked printed page 39. Proposed synthesis uses Ricks on page 39 only.
sources.sourceUnit: One federal hearing; selected tribal-authored testimony

sources.title: After More Than 170 Years, Siletz Tribe To Reclaim Ceded Land
sources.annotation: Interviews and a Siletz council statement connect prospective coastal land return with community memory and stewardship. The article still describes transfer as pending. Its compressed historical chronology is not used to date earlier reservation reductions.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete substantive article, lines 63–106, including the pending-transaction paragraph. No photographs, precise parcel location, legal title conclusions or invitation-only access arrangements are reproduced.

sources.title: Alsea Texts and Myths: methodological and vocabulary introductions
sources.publisher: Bureau of American Ethnology, Government Printing Office; public scan hosted by Internet Archive
sources.annotation: Frachtenberg’s historical edition records contributions from named Alsea speakers and explains editorial and vocabulary methods. Read its early twentieth-century judgments critically. Neither its predictions about language nor its narrow surviving sample establishes disappearance of Alsea people or the limits of community knowledge.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual public scan-derived OCR read for printed pages 9–11 and 243–245; title and 1920 imprint checked. No full-book, narrative or recording review. OCR can corrupt transcription. Smithsonian PDF was size-blocked by web reader and returned403 through ordinary download; this lawful public copy supplied actual text.
sources.author: Leo J. Frachtenberg; named Alsea contributors discussed in the introduction

inspectedSubresources.title: Public scan-derived text: methodological introductions
inspectedSubresources.scope: Printed pages9–11 and243–245 inspected; other contents not reviewed.

sources.title: The Alsea Noun Phrase
sources.author: Eugene Buckley
sources.publisher: Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics, University of Kansas; full article copy in ERIC
sources.citation: Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics 14(2), Studies in Native American Languages V, pp. 20–36.
sources.annotation: Focused analysis of Alsea noun phrases, possession and small grammatical elements whose placement depends on phrase structure. Buckley explicitly identifies gaps in the recorded evidence. Selected descriptive and analytical pages were read; this is not a complete teaching grammar or a present-use survey.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual article, printed pp. 20–22,26–28,33–36 (ERIC PDF pp. 2–4,8–10,15–18), read in extracted text. Includes descriptive examples, formal analysis, evidentiary limits and notes; not just the ERIC abstract.

inspectedSubresources.scope: Publisher article metadata, author, DOI, 1989 year, 20–36 page range and CC BY 4.0 license statement.

sources.title: Temporal Boundaries in Alsea
sources.author: Eugene Buckley
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the Berkeley Linguistics Society; online publisher Linguistic Society of America
sources.citation: Proceedings of the Fourteenth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society, pp. 10–22.
sources.annotation: Proposes an analysis of how Alsea verbs mark events' beginnings, endings and resulting states. Comparisons with English translations show why context matters. Selected scanned pages, including the conclusion and source notes, were visually read; historical linguistic analysis does not establish contemporary speaker numbers.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual scanned article, printed pp. 10–12 and 17–21 (full PDF pp. 2–4 and 9–13), visually read after rendering. Publisher cover and article metadata also inspected. Intervening pp. 13–16 and final notes/reference page 22 were not read.

inspectedSubresources.scope: Author, DOI,1988 proceedings and 10–22 range; portal lists publication date 1988-10-25. The source card conservatively records the proceedings year.

sources.title: MS 2516: Alsea and Lower Umpqua texts and notes
sources.annotation: Finding aid distinguishes Alsea notebooks from a Lower Umpqua grammatical index and records corrections to notebook authorship. This describes holdings and research routes; it does not turn every linked manuscript into an inspected work.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual finding-aid summary and scope/content notes read. No linked manuscript images or recordings inspected. Supporting reference outside the substantive target.

sources.title: Alsea (Alcea)
sources.annotation: Primarily an article about the modern town. Its short opening provides regional historical orientation; retain as supporting reading, outside substantive Alsea depth. The logging history is town history, not an account of all Alsea people.

relationshipNote: Alsea is one ancestral people within the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians. The Alsea Subagency administered several distinct peoples. Siletz Dee-ni (Athabaskan/Dené) teaching resources do not represent the Alsea language.
researchGaps: Seek further specifically Alsea family and community perspectives, including contemporary language relationships and cultural practice, without substituting generic Siletz activities.
Read the final1875 enacted provision and the original1865 order directly; a Senate debate is not the enacted law, and authorial summaries can contain chronology errors.
The edited Coos testimony concerns shared reservation history; its witnesses must not be relabeled Alsea or used to fill Alsea-specific depth.
Historical linguistic studies draw on overlapping older corpora. Their analysis and transcription limits do not establish current language use or disappearance of people.
The October2026 coastal-transfer report describes an ongoing transaction. Completion, title and present access require later verified evidence.
Historical photographs are research leads for a later design phase; attribution, rights and cultural context must be checked before any reuse. Community review remains open.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Eleven substantive works or conservatively grouped collections were inspected, with three supporting cards outside the target. Actual tribal lessons and history, an Indigenous historian, primary debate and testimony, Native reporting and selected linguistic studies support a useful introduction. The bounded search also found access failures, duplicate routes and broader contextual material that was not promoted to reach twelve. Initial coverage supports continuing alphabetically while specific family, cultural and primary-record gaps remain open.
remainingLimits: The twelve-source quantity target has not been reached; adequacy is a separate dated judgment.
Selected passages, confederated context and shared historical corpora have explicit limits; research is not complete or community endorsed.

evidenceNotes: Related Siletz history pages count as one unit; selected curriculum lessons count as one collection. The Coos-focused claims testimony, modern-town overview and archival finding aid remain outside the substantive target.

The1865 executive action is distinct from the1875 congressional reduction. Nineteenth-century administrative language does not establish consent. The1954 termination law and1956 implementation are distinct from continuing identity and1977 restoration.
No sacred narratives, historical photographs, precise sensitive places, current speaker totals or unverified legal outcomes are reproduced.

name: Alutiiq
overview: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq people have coastal homelands spanning Prince William Sound, the outer Kenai Peninsula, Kodiak Archipelago, and Alaska Peninsula. Community-preferred names vary across this region. Kodiak's community-governed Alutiiq Museum connects archaeological history, language learning, village histories, and present institutions, offering an especially substantial account of the Kodiak part of this wider world.

sections.title: Alutiiq, Sugpiaq, and the history of naming
sections.text: Sugpiaq is a traditional self-designation, with Sugpiat its plural; Alutiit is the plural of Alutiiq. Alutiiq developed through the local pronunciation of Russian Aleuty and was deliberately embraced by Kodiak cultural leaders during the heritage movement. Some people prefer Sugpiaq, others Alutiiq or Aleut. The museum emphasizes personal and regional choice. Russian use of Aleut for several peoples explains historical confusion, but does not make Alutiiq/Sugpiaq identical with Unangax̂ people of the Aleutian Islands.

sections.title: Deep coastal history
sections.text: The museum's archaeological synthesis traces Kodiak settlement back at least 7,800 years. Archaeologists use Ocean Bay, Kachemak, and Koniag traditions to describe changing technologies and ways of living. Early sea-mammal hunting and cod fishing were followed by increasingly intensive salmon harvesting, storage, and exchange. Later communities included large multi-room houses shared by related families. These are archaeological period labels within a long Indigenous history; they are not names of three successive modern tribal governments.

sections.title: Russian conquest and coerced work
sections.text: Russian merchant Grigorii Shelikhov arrived in 1784 seeking a fur-trading enterprise dependent on Native labor. His forces attacked people sheltering at Awa’uq, also called Refuge Rock, killing many and taking hostages. Forts, hostage-taking, coerced work, hunger, and introduced diseases transformed Kodiak communities. The museum treats the assault as a decisive loss of control over the homeland. Its account also connects later village consolidation with the devastating colonial period, placing settlement changes within that history of violence.

sections.title: Village histories and continuing ties
sections.text: Kodiak village histories differ substantially. At Karluk, salmon supported ancestral settlement and later commercial canneries, whose intensive harvests depleted runs. At Afognak, the 1964 earthquake's tsunamis damaged buildings and contaminated wells, leading residents to relocate to Port Lions. Yet Afognak remains a place of harvesting, visiting, and tribal culture camps. Kaguyak likewise retained community and council connections after physical resettlement. A village's loss of permanent residents therefore cannot be read as the end of its people or their relationship to that place.

sections.title: Language suppression and renewed learning
sections.text: Alutiiq is also called Alutiit’stun or Sugt’stun, reflecting speakers' preferred identities. Nineteenth-century Alutiiq writers used Cyrillic letters in religious translations. Later American schools punished children for speaking Alutiiq, and families reduced transmission to protect them from mistreatment. Elders, tribes, and educators have subsequently documented speech, mentored learners, developed vocabulary for contemporary life, and created dictionaries, recordings, games, and classes. The museum's language history locates renewed learning within community action, rather than treating reduced fluency as cultural disappearance.

sections.title: Tribes and corporations have different roles
sections.text: Kodiak Alutiiq people participate in distinct tribal governments, Native corporations, and nonprofit organizations. The museum's directory includes the Sun’aq Tribe of Kodiak, Native Village of Afognak, Alutiiq Tribe of Old Harbor, and other governments. Tribes exercise sovereignty and provide services; corporations established through the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act manage assets and benefits for shareholders and descendants. One person may have relationships with several institutions. Corporate affiliation is consequently not a substitute for identifying the relevant tribal government.

sources.title: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq People
sources.annotation: Community-governed museum introduction maps the wider Alutiiq/Sugpiaq homeland and links an identity film, cultural resources, and language material. Its institutional base is Kodiak, within a broader regional people.

sources.title: Alutiiq — What Is in a Name?
sources.annotation: Explains Alutiiq, Sugpiaq, plural forms, and language names through community preferences and colonial naming history. Particularly useful for respecting variation without equating Alutiiq with Unangax̂.

sources.title: Our Stories
sources.annotation: Introduces Ocean Bay, Kachemak, and Koniag archaeological traditions and links museum films, an eBook, and focused historical lessons. The deep-history text provides the evidence summarized here; linked films were not transcribed.

sources.title: Awa’uq — Refuge Rock: Conquest of Kodiak
sources.annotation: One-page museum history of the 1784 assault, hostage-taking, forced labor, and colonial disruption. Links further scholarship by Gordon Pullar and Lydia Black; avoids requiring readers to treat uncertain casualty estimates as precise counts.

sources.title: 20th Century Kodiak Alutiiq Villages
sources.annotation: Individual histories and photographs distinguish Kodiak villages, commercial fishing, disasters, relocation, and continuing place-based relationships. Includes Afognak/Port Lions, Karluk, Kaguyak, and other communities.

sources.title: Language History: Alutiit’stun — Like an Alutiiq
sources.annotation: Connects visual communication, early writing, multilingual colonial life, English-only schooling, and elder-led learning. Undated present-day speaker totals are not used in this profile.

sources.title: Tribes and Corporations
sources.annotation: Explains different roles of sovereign tribes, ANCSA corporations, and nonprofits and lists Kodiak tribal governments. Shareholder statistics are dated September 2022 and are not presented as current figures here.

relationshipNote: Sugpiaq (entry 362) and Alutiiq overlap as community self-designations rather than representing two wholly separate peoples. Individual preferences vary. Unangax̂/Aleut is a distinct people and language despite colonial use of Aleut across regions.
researchGaps: Add further community-authored perspectives and specialist scholarship for a fuller account.
Seek community review and expand topics not yet covered in this introduction.

name: Amuzgo
overview: Amuzgo communities live in the adjoining regions of Guerrero and Oaxaca in southern Mexico. The name covers a people and several closely related Oto-Manguean languages, with local self-designations and histories. Xochistlahuaca/Suljaa’, Tlacoachistlahuaca, San Pedro Amuzgos, and Santa María Ipalapa offer different settings for understanding language, textiles, land, and community organization.

sections.title: Homelands and community-specific names
sections.text: The historical Amuzgo region lies in the Sierra Madre del Sur near the Pacific coast at the Guerrero–Oaxaca border. Mexico's cultural information system identifies language communities on both sides of that state boundary. It records ñomndaa at Xochistlahuaca and ñonndaa or jñon’ndaa at San Pedro Amuzgos, illustrating why a single standardized spelling cannot replace local usage. Amuzgo is a wider people and language-group label; these named towns and their institutions must be identified separately when discussing particular decisions or events.

sections.title: Oral history, colonialism, and land
sections.text: The government's historical synthesis records oral traditions of origins in island lands at sea, followed by movement toward the coast and inland. This is explicitly an account of oral history rather than a dated archaeological migration sequence. It also describes colonial exploitation, evangelization, dispossession, and the role of Xochistlahuaca as an administrative and religious center from 1563. Land-recovery struggles in the twentieth century led to an ejido restitution in 1933. Those local events should not be treated as the complete history of every Amuzgo settlement.

sections.title: Related languages, distinct varieties
sections.text: The national cultural catalog identifies four Amuzgo varieties: northern, southern, lower eastern, and upper eastern, each associated with one or more self-designations. They belong to the Oto-Manguean family. INALI's courtesy-phrase resource specifically represents northern Amuzgo/nomndaa from Xochistlahuaca and Tlacoachistlahuaca, with text and voice credited to Yanneth Guerrero Valentín. It makes pronunciation and ordinary social exchanges accessible while demonstrating that a learning resource may represent a particular variety rather than every Amuzgo-speaking community.

sections.title: Textiles as knowledge, work, and identity
sections.text: Amuzgo huipil-making connects agricultural materials, skilled labor, design, and community identity. The cultural heritage inventory describes growing coyuchi cotton, spinning with spindle and whorl, dyeing, preparing a backstrap loom, and brocading designs while weaving. Separate woven panels are joined to make a garment; flowers, animals, and geometric figures appear among its designs. Huipiles participate in weddings, ceremonies, and other life events, while artisans also produce garments and household textiles for sale. The 2012 inventory is evidence for techniques and significance, not a current survey of all weavers' practices.

sections.title: Community communication and cultural agency
sections.text: Radio Ñomndaa's own account identifies the station at Suljaa’ as an Indigenous, autonomous community medium independent of governments, parties, and religious organizations. It presents communication, access to information, cultural strengthening, and respect for other peoples as central purposes. This self-description adds a community voice alongside government reference pages and shows cultural work through media as well as material arts. The site's historical presentation should not be used to guarantee a present broadcasting schedule, live stream, or the political views of every Amuzgo person.

sources.title: Amuzgo — Lenguas indígenas
sources.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural
sources.annotation: Names four language varieties, gives local self-designations, and describes the Guerrero–Oaxaca borderland. Dated 2020 but incorporating older census geography; undated headline speaker counts are not used here.

sources.title: Amuzgos — Pueblos indígenas
sources.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural
sources.annotation: Historical overview distinguishes oral origin traditions, colonial changes, Xochistlahuaca's role, and twentieth-century land restitution. Also introduces arts and local festivals; its summary is not a substitute for individual community histories.

sources.title: Nomndaa — Prontuario de frases de cortesía
sources.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas; text and voice by Yanneth Guerrero Valentín
sources.annotation: Text-and-voice courtesy phrases explicitly identified as northern Amuzgo from Xochistlahuaca and Tlacoachistlahuaca. The recorded variety is specified, and dated 2010 speaker figures are not generalized to the present.

sources.title: Huipiles Amuzgos: tejido en telar de cintura y brocado con hilos de algodón
sources.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural
sources.annotation: 2012 heritage inventory describing cotton preparation, backstrap weaving, brocade, garment assembly, and huipiles' social significance across Guerrero and Oaxaca. Its older risk assessments are not reported as current conditions.

sources.title: ¿Qué es Radio Ñomndaa? — La Palabra del Agua
sources.annotation: The Suljaa’ community radio project's self-description articulates cultural, communication, and autonomy goals in its own voice. This historical website is used for the project's stated purposes, not verification of current stream availability or schedules.

relationshipNote: Amuzgo is a wider people and closely related language grouping spanning Guerrero and Oaxaca. Local self-designations, language varieties, towns, municipal institutions, and autonomous community projects should not be conflated into one government.
researchGaps: Add further community-authored perspectives and specialist scholarship for a fuller account.
Seek community review and expand topics not yet covered in this introduction.

name: Anishinaabe
overview: Anishinaabe is a broad identity expressed through related peoples, languages, families, and sovereign communities across the Great Lakes and beyond. Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi histories are central to the Three Fires relationship. Contemporary institutions such as Ontario's Anishinabek Nation and the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission represent particular communities rather than every Anishinaabe person.

sections.title: Related peoples and particular governments
sections.text: Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi maintain distinct identities within an interconnected history. The Anishinabek Nation traces political roots to the Three Fires Confederacy, whose councils served diplomatic and military purposes in the Great Lakes. Its present Ontario organization and the individual First Nations it represents are specific political bodies. On the U.S. side, GLIFWC serves particular Ojibwe bands. These examples show why a shared Anishinaabe identity cannot by itself identify someone's government, treaty, citizenship, or community protocol.

sections.title: Oral tradition, migration, and the Three Fires
sections.text: Citizen Potawatomi Nation's Cultural Heritage Center presents the Seven Fires Prophecy as part of its own oral history. Its account connects Neshnabek ancestors, a westward journey, and arrival in the Great Lakes where wild rice grew on the water. It also describes the related Potawatomi, Odawa, and Ojibwe peoples and the Three Fires Council. This community interpretation links past experience with responsibilities toward the future; it should be read as a situated oral tradition, rather than converted into a universal, precisely dated migration timetable.

sections.title: An example of contemporary constitutional governance
sections.text: The Anishinabek Nation's Anishinaabe Chi-Naaknigewin was proclaimed in 2012. It defines the participating nation through First Nations that proclaimed and signed the constitution and grounds government in Anishinaabe law, a clan-based framework, and seven sacred gifts. It provides for a Grand Council with advisory Elders', Women's, and Youth councils and states that individual First Nation laws take precedence where they exist. This is a particular exercise of collective self-government that also recognizes constituent communities, not a constitution binding all Anishinaabe nations.

sections.title: Treaties and continuing relationships to homelands
sections.text: GLIFWC's member bands are connected to the 1836, 1837, 1842, and 1854 treaties and their ceded territories in the Great Lakes. The commission explains that signatories retained hunting, fishing, gathering, and self-government rights as part of their agreements with the United States. Its work connects treaty implementation with resource stewardship and future generations. Such rights arise through particular treaties and peoples: this regional example should not be treated as a uniform legal rule for every Anishinaabe community in either country.

sections.title: Knowledge, harvesting, and environmental change
sections.text: GLIFWC describes Anishinaabe ways of knowing through detailed understanding of fish and wildlife, plants, seasonal change, and harvesting. Stories, songs, place names, and traditions transmit localized knowledge across generations. The commission combines this knowledge with contemporary science and policy, including interviews about changing conditions affecting wild rice, birch, cedar, berries, and other beings. Its approach treats language, ecological relationships, and tribal sovereignty as connected responsibilities, while recognizing that knowledge is grounded in particular landscapes and communities.

sections.title: Language resources and regional variation
sections.text: Anishinaabemowin is among the names used for Ojibwe, but its use and scope depend on the speaker and institution. The Ojibwe People's Dictionary specifically centers Central Southwestern Ojibwe from Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Canadian border-lakes communities. Its double-vowel writing system, speaker-attributed recordings, and regional labels make language differences visible. The Anishinabek constitution uses Anishinaabemowin inclusively for its peoples' languages. Comparing these explicit definitions prevents an Ojibwe dictionary or an Ontario institutional term from being mistaken for a single uniform language standard across all related peoples.

sources.title: About Anishinabek Nation
sources.annotation: The Ontario organization explains its relationship to the Union of Ontario Indians, its member First Nations, and Three Fires political history. A specific institutional account rather than an exhaustive definition of all Anishinaabe peoples.

sources.title: Prophetic wisdom: The Seven Fires sets tribe on path to its future
sources.annotation: 2018 account of the nation's Seven Fires exhibit, featuring cultural staff explanations of oral tradition, migration, wild rice, colonial disruption, and renewal. Its specific Potawatomi perspective is identified rather than generalized to every community.

sources.title: Anishinaabe Chi-Naaknigewin — Anishinabek Nation Constitution
sources.annotation: Primary constitutional text proclaimed June 6, 2012, defining participating First Nations, language, councils, clan governance, and relationships between laws. The text's institutional scope is essential to its interpretation.

sources.title: The Commission — Ojibwe Ceded Territories
sources.publisher: Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission
sources.annotation: Intertribal commission introduction identifies member-band websites, relevant treaties, and reserved harvesting and self-government relationships. A community institutional explanation, not advice about an individual's legal eligibility.

sources.title: Indigenous Knowledge
sources.publisher: Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission
sources.annotation: Explains locally grounded Anishinaabe knowledge and its integration with resource science and policy. Includes discussion of interviews, environmental observations, and the transmission of knowledge through language and cultural forms.

sources.title: About the Ojibwe Language
sources.publisher: Ojibwe People's Dictionary; University of Minnesota collaborators
sources.annotation: Specifies the dictionary's Central Southwestern Ojibwe focus, writing system, speaker voices, and regional marking. Supports meaningful language exploration while keeping its geographical scope clear; old speaker counts are not used here.

relationshipNote: Anishinaabe is a wider and context-dependent identity, linked here to Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi. The Three Fires relationship, Ontario's Anishinabek Nation, GLIFWC, and individual sovereign communities have different scopes and are not interchangeable names.
researchGaps: Add further community-authored perspectives and specialist scholarship for a fuller account.
Seek community review and expand topics not yet covered in this introduction.

name: Anishininew
overview: Anishininew, also written Anisininew, identifies distinct peoples and communities in northeastern Manitoba and northwestern Ontario. Island Lake nations emphasize their own identity rather than the outside label Oji-Cree. Their histories connect family harvesting territories, treaty relationships, language education and contemporary institutions controlled by the communities themselves.

sections.title: Names, identity and community scope
sections.text: Wasagamack Anisininew Nation’s 2024 community guide explicitly rejects describing its people as part Cree and part Ojibwe. It recalls an Island Lake declaration in 2018 and a wider gathering of Anisininew nations in February 2024 affirming a distinct identity. The guide also explains that Oji-Cree can be offensive locally. Spellings vary across community publications; the names used by the particular nation should guide discussion. Island Lake is an important regional focus, rather than the full extent of Anishininew peoplehood.

sections.title: Island Lake homelands and treaty history
sections.text: Garden Hill, Wasagamack, St. Theresa Point and Red Sucker Lake share an Island Lake history while maintaining separate communities. Wasagamack’s school history locates the community on Island Lake’s western shore and identifies its participation in the 1909 adhesion to Treaty 5. The community’s own guide dates that signing to August 13 at Old Post on Linklater Island and describes treaty promises as unfinished obligations. This local account makes land, education and harvesting central to the treaty relationship, rather than treating the signing as the end of Indigenous authority.

sections.title: Northern Ontario histories have their own institutions
sections.text: Kitchenuhmaykoosib Inninuwug’s history describes Anishinewuk family groups managing customary hunting territories around Big Trout Lake, with headmen representing clans. Summer gatherings renewed relationships through ceremonies, teaching, feasts, exchange and trade. Its account dates the local Treaty 9 adhesion to July 5, 1929 and records an understanding that the people would retain control over customary lands and resources. Later settlements developed their own administrations. These histories show why a Manitoba regional council cannot stand in for every community identified by a related name.

sections.title: Language and education in community hands
sections.text: Garden Hill Anisininew Nation High School describes teaching through English while integrating Anisinimowin, the Island Lake dialect, and cultural learning. Elders and Knowledge Keepers contribute stories, teachings and perspectives alongside the provincial curriculum. Wasagamack First Nation School similarly describes traditional learning and Elder guidance as part of schooling under its own education authority. These are concrete institutions in which language and community knowledge remain part of young people’s education. Their distinct programs should not be reduced to a single generic account of northern Indigenous schooling.

sections.title: Health, food and collective self-determination
sections.text: The four Island Lake First Nations created and govern Four Arrows Regional Health Authority. Its institutional history traces planning in 1999, formal authorization in 2000 and responsibility for regional health services in 2001. Its Kimeechiminan food program connects health with language, land, cultural teaching and food sharing. Projects described on the program’s site include gardening, harvesting, food skills and a Garden Hill food enterprise. This approach treats food sovereignty as community leadership over food systems and relationships, alongside access to nutritious groceries.

sources.title: Welcome to Wasagamack Anisininew Nation (2024 community guide)
sources.publisher: Wasagamack Anisininew Nation / Teach For Canada
sources.annotation: Community welcome signed by Chief and Council, with a timeline and Elder interviews. Pages 3–6 explain treaty history and preferred identity; its local naming guidance matters when encountering Oji-Cree in older sources.

sources.title: Wasagamack First Nation School: community and school profile
sources.annotation: School account of Wasagamack’s location, Treaty 5 relationship, education authority and traditional teaching. It uses older language terminology; compare its naming with the nation’s 2024 guide.

sources.title: About Garden Hill Anisininew Nation High School
sources.publisher: Garden Hill Anisininew Nation High School
sources.annotation: Explains how the school integrates Anisinimowin, cultural learning and Elder participation with secondary education. It identifies the four Island Lake communities while remaining specific to Garden Hill’s school.

sources.title: About FARHA
sources.annotation: The regional health organization’s own history of its creation and governance by the four Island Lake First Nations. Useful for understanding practical cooperation between distinct community governments.

sources.title: Kimeechiminan – Food Security
sources.annotation: Connects food security with Indigenous leadership, language, land and teaching. Includes examples of food sharing, gardening, harvesting and the Garden Hill Meechim project; project descriptions are not a dated inventory of current operations.

sources.title: KI History
sources.annotation: First Nation account of family territories, seasonal gatherings, the 1929 Treaty 9 adhesion and later political organization around Big Trout Lake. Its presentation of oral treaty understandings complements written Crown records.

relationshipNote: Anishininew/Anisininew is not an interchangeable label for Cree or Anishinaabe. Island Lake’s four nations are one regional grouping; community names and spellings in northern Ontario also need their own context.

name: Apache
overview: Apache is an umbrella name connecting distinct peoples, languages and sovereign governments, rather than one political nation. Community histories encompass the Southwest, southern Plains and northern Mexico. The Apache Tribe of Oklahoma, Mescalero Apache Tribe, San Carlos Apache Tribe and Yavapai-Apache Nation illustrate different histories within this broader field.

sections.title: A broad name with distinct political meanings
sections.text: The Apache Tribe of Oklahoma, also called Plains Apache, is a distinct community rather than another name for all Apache peoples. The Oklahoma Historical Society explains that its people maintain a separate linguistic and cultural identity despite long associations with Kiowa and other Plains nations. The Yavapai-Apache Nation offers another important distinction: it joins two peoples, Yavapai and Apache, in one government. Its Apache people identify as Dil’zhe’e, while its Yavapai people identify as Wipuhk’a’bah. A shared government and a broad ethnographic name therefore describe different kinds of relationships.

sections.title: Land use was diverse and place-specific
sections.text: San Carlos Apache history describes seasonal movement between river valleys and higher country, combining hunting and plant gathering with fields of corn, squash and beans. Acorns and mescal were important foods. The Plains Apache in Oklahoma followed a different regional trajectory: the Oklahoma Historical Society describes mobile bison hunting on the Great Plains, followed by confinement to western Oklahoma reservation lands from 1867 to allotment in 1901. These different settings and histories shaped livelihoods. Accounts centered entirely on warfare miss the agricultural knowledge and varied uses of landscapes described in these sources.

sections.title: Confinement and exile reshaped communities
sections.text: San Carlos’s history explains how settler pressure, the 1871 Camp Grant Massacre and reservation confinement restricted movement and separated children from families through assimilationist schooling. Fort Sill Apache history follows a different sequence: Chiricahua people were imprisoned in Florida and Alabama before their transfer to Oklahoma in 1894. Some later joined Mescalero; others insisted on lands they had been promised near Fort Sill and were released and resettled on allotments in 1914. Their present locations must be understood through these forced movements.

sections.title: Mescalero and Lipan histories cross the border
sections.text: The Mescalero Apache Tribe identifies Mescalero, Lipan and Chiricahua as its three constituent groups. Its history dates the reservation’s establishment by executive order to May 29, 1873, with Lipan arrivals from northern Chihuahua around 1903 and Chiricahua arrivals in 1913. The Lipan Apache Tribe’s own account also follows communities that remained in Texas and moved between Texas and Mexico. Membership in Mescalero consequently does not encompass every Lipan community. The international boundary cuts across histories of refuge, dispossession, kinship and survival.

sections.title: Language and cultural transmission
sections.text: The San Carlos Apache Language Preservation Program operates under tribal council direction. Its work includes Elder interviews, collecting place names and knowledge of plants and animals, teaching classes, and developing resources for families and young people. Mescalero’s cultural account places language, Elder guidance and family responsibility within continuing community life; it describes the girls’ coming-of-age ceremony as a major collective commitment. These examples belong to particular communities and should not be presented as identical practices across all Apache peoples.

sections.title: Governments and public institutions today
sections.text: Tribal websites also document contemporary government and services. The Yavapai-Apache Nation lists courts, health care, housing, youth services and educational support, and explains how economic enterprises help fund them. The Fort Sill Apache Tribe’s history records constitutional organization, land acquisition in its ancestral region and a New Mexico reservation proclamation in 2011. These institutions demonstrate continuing political life after confinement and displacement. They also provide separate starting points for studying each government’s own citizenship, laws, priorities and relationship with its homeland.

sources.title: Apache Tribe of Oklahoma, by Dianna Everett
sources.annotation: Historical reference distinguishes the Apache Tribe of Oklahoma from other Apache communities and emphasizes its own linguistic and cultural identity. Its demographic figures and program descriptions are dated and are not used as current measurements.

sources.title: Yavapai-Apache Nation
sources.annotation: Nation-published explanation of its two distinct peoples, their self-names, Verde Valley communities and governmental services. Population figures on the page are explicitly from 2019 and are not used here as current counts.

sources.title: Our History
sources.annotation: Community account of seasonal food production, settler encroachment, the Camp Grant Massacre, confinement and boarding schools. Read it for San Carlos and Western Apache perspectives, with attention to the communities named.

sources.title: Fort Sill Apache History
sources.annotation: Tribal history of Chiricahua imprisonment, relocation, the split between Mescalero and Oklahoma settlement, and later land and political recognition. Distinguishes this government from the neighboring Apache Tribe of Oklahoma.

sources.title: Our Culture
sources.annotation: Explains the tribe’s Mescalero, Lipan and Chiricahua composition, reservation formation and cultural teachings. Its public discussion of ceremony and respectful behavior is a Mescalero account, not permission to generalize across all Apache peoples.

sources.title: Our Sacred History: Who We Are
sources.annotation: The Lipan Apache Tribe’s own history of Texas homelands, cross-border refuge, surviving communities and present government. Useful alongside Mescalero history to avoid treating all Lipan descendants as one governmental membership.

sources.title: Apache Language Preservation
sources.annotation: Program description covering Elder interviews, teaching, place-name and ecological documentation, family outreach and resources. Its specific institutional activities provide a grounded account of language work.

relationshipNote: Apache is a wider grouping. Plains/Kiowa Apache, Mescalero, Lipan, Chiricahua and Western Apache histories overlap without being interchangeable. The Fort Sill Apache Tribe and Apache Tribe of Oklahoma are separate governments; Yavapai is a distinct people within the Yavapai-Apache Nation.
