name: Apalachee
overview: Apalachee history connects the farming towns of north Florida with surviving descendants in Louisiana. Spanish missions, forced labor, warfare and enslavement transformed their homelands, but the destruction of mission settlements did not end Apalachee peoplehood. The Talimali Band’s community work provides an essential present-day perspective alongside archaeology and colonial records.

sections.title: Homelands, farming towns and political organization
sections.text: Mission San Luis’s historical interpretation places Apalachee territory between the Ochlockonee and Aucilla rivers in north Florida. Communities participated in a wider southeastern world of farming, mound building and exchange. The museum describes matrilineal clans and a hierarchy of local leaders, with a principal leader called the holata. These institutions predated the Spanish settlement at San Luis. Apalachee history therefore begins with organized Indigenous communities and their relationships to land and neighboring peoples, rather than with the establishment of European missions.

sections.title: Alliance and coercion in the Spanish mission period
sections.text: Apalachee leaders sought closer relations with Spanish authorities and requested friars in the early seventeenth century. Permanent missions began in 1633; San Luis moved to its later Tallahassee site in 1656. It became a center of both Apalachee leadership and Spanish administration. Relations also involved coercion: the repartimiento labor system took men away from their farms to transport goods, build structures and work for Spanish enterprises, sometimes for weeks or months. Spanish seizure of materials and land further strained an alliance that had never meant equal power.

sections.title: The 1704 diaspora and the path to Louisiana
sections.text: English colonial attacks and their Indigenous allies devastated the mission system, killing and enslaving residents. In 1704, Apalachee and Spanish residents evacuated and burned San Luis rather than leave it for approaching enemies. Survivors followed several routes, including refuge near St. Augustine and movement toward French-controlled Mobile. The museum timeline places a later move from Mobile toward Louisiana’s Red River in 1763–1764. These migrations explain the connection between Florida ancestral towns and Louisiana descendants; an abandoned archaeological site should not be mistaken for the disappearance of a people.

sections.title: What archaeology adds, and whose records survive
sections.text: Excavations at Mission San Luis study homes, public buildings, refuse and other remains to reconstruct everyday life. Pottery is particularly revealing: Apalachee-made vessels sometimes adopted forms associated with imported Spanish objects, including handles and ring bases. Food remains and gardens likewise show exchange and adaptation. The museum acknowledges that much written evidence comes from Spanish officials and friars working through Apalachee translators. Reading those texts beside material evidence and descendant perspectives helps distinguish colonial descriptions from the people’s own historical experience.

sections.title: Continuing community, education and public memory
sections.text: The Talimali Band of the Apalachee Indians of Louisiana identifies itself as a continuing descendant community based in Pineville. Its public account describes cultural preservation, educational outreach, archaeological consultation and scholarships for young people. It dates nonprofit incorporation to 1995 and its filing for federal recognition to 1996; a filing should not be confused with a recognition determination. Its community-project pages also describe plans for village and museum expansion. These are examples of contemporary community building, complementing the historical story told at the Florida museum.

sources.title: Who Are the Apalachee Indians Today?
sources.publisher: Talimali Band of the Apalachee Indians of Louisiana
sources.annotation: Descendant community’s account of its Louisiana roots, historical continuity, cultural preservation and educational programs. Its distinction between a recognition application and continuing community identity is useful alongside older histories.

sources.title: The Apalachee
sources.publisher: Mission San Luis / Florida Department of State
sources.annotation: Museum interpretation of territory, agricultural communities, matrilineal clans and leadership. Used for specific Apalachee institutions; broad archaeological-era generalizations on the page should not replace community history.

sources.title: Mission San Luis
sources.publisher: Mission San Luis / Florida Department of State
sources.annotation: Details requests for friars, mission establishment, relocation and colonial labor demands. Particularly helpful for understanding both Indigenous diplomacy and unequal power within the Spanish alliance.

sources.title: End of the Mission System
sources.publisher: Mission San Luis / Florida Department of State
sources.annotation: Explains English attacks, enslavement, San Luis’s evacuation and multiple survivor routes. Its older language about people fading away is not adopted here; descendant continuity must be read alongside it.

sources.title: Timeline
sources.publisher: Mission San Luis / Florida Department of State
sources.annotation: Provides dates for mission developments, the 1704 destruction, the 1763–1764 move toward Louisiana and later contact between descendants and museum researchers. Useful for separating successive migrations.

sources.title: Archaeology
sources.publisher: Mission San Luis / Florida Department of State
sources.annotation: Explains excavation evidence, Spanish archival records, gardens and pottery adaptation. Makes the evidentiary basis of the reconstructed mission visible rather than presenting the museum as an unchanged surviving village.

sources.title: Apalachee Community Projects
sources.publisher: Talimali Band of the Apalachee Indians of Louisiana
sources.annotation: Community descriptions of village expansion, museum planning and relief work. These are projects described by the Band, with some entries explicitly historical; they are not independent confirmation that every proposed project is completed.

relationshipNote: Apalachee names an Indigenous people; San Luis de Talimali was a particular ancestral town and mission. The Talimali Band is a contemporary Louisiana descendant community, whose organization and recognition history should be distinguished from colonial population labels.

name: Arapaho
overview: Arapaho people, identified as Hinono’ei in the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes’ account, maintain distinct northern and southern political communities. Their history includes wide-ranging Plains homelands, alliance with Cheyenne people, violent dispossession and continuing language and cultural work. Northern Arapaho institutions at Wind River and the Oklahoma government require separate attention.

sections.title: Homelands and northern and southern communities
sections.text: The Arapaho Project describes historical lands extending across the central Plains and toward the Rocky Mountains, rather than a homeland confined to one modern state. In the nineteenth century, northern and southern groups centered increasingly on the North Platte and Arkansas river valleys. Bison hunting, horses and trade were central to life on the Plains. The history emphasizes alliance with Cheyenne people. Northern Arapaho settled at Wind River in 1878; Southern Arapaho histories led to west-central Oklahoma, producing different reservation and governmental experiences.

sections.title: Sand Creek and the consequences of dispossession
sections.text: On November 29, 1864, Colorado volunteer soldiers attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho encampment at Sand Creek. The National Park Service identifies many of the victims as women, children and elderly people. This massacre forms part of the violent process through which settlers and governments displaced communities from their lands. Its history also survives through families. Descendants and tribal leaders undertook oral-history investigations that helped identify the massacre site, alongside documentary and archaeological work. The national historic site opened in 2007 after that collaborative research.

sections.title: Separate governments and contemporary public services
sections.text: The Northern Arapaho Tribe’s official site places it on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming and provides access to its Business Council and tribal codes. Its department directory includes family services, water and sewer operations, vocational rehabilitation and immersion education. The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes government in Oklahoma presents executive, legislative, judicial and Tribal Council branches; the Tribal Council includes adult tribal members. These public institutions show why references to an Arapaho cultural community must be distinguished from the powers and organization of a particular sovereign government.

sections.title: Language learning across generations
sections.text: Arapaho belongs to the Algonquian language family, with a distinctive history of sound change that makes it differ considerably from many relatives. The Arapaho Project links grammar, pronunciation, stories, lessons and dictionaries for learners. The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes describe community and online classes, youth language outreach, Elder participation and an adult Master Apprentice program. Northern Arapaho’s directory separately lists immersion education at Ethete. These initiatives involve teaching and relationships among generations, extending beyond the preservation of recordings or written materials alone.

sections.title: Cultural authority, repatriation and historical interpretation
sections.text: The Cheyenne and Arapaho Culture Program includes representatives working on the return of ancestral remains and funerary belongings from institutions. It also includes Sand Creek representatives who work with the National Park Service on how the massacre is presented publicly. Together with descendants’ role in identifying the site, this demonstrates that communities participate in deciding how history is researched, cared for and explained. Their cultural work connects living families, ancestral places, language teaching and obligations toward earlier generations, rather than treating heritage as a collection of detached museum objects.

sources.title: Language and Culture
sources.annotation: Tribal account of Arapaho identity and history, language classes, Elder involvement, cultural work and Sand Creek representatives. Distinguishes Arapaho and Cheyenne languages within their shared Oklahoma government.

sources.title: Northern Arapaho Tribe
sources.annotation: Official northern government entry point with Wind River location, Business Council, tribal codes and departmental navigation. Use it to distinguish this government from the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma.

sources.title: Department Listings
sources.annotation: Government directory naming practical services, including family support, water and sewer operations and immersion at Ethete. This is evidence of specific institutions, rather than a general cultural summary.

sources.title: Government
sources.annotation: Explains the functions of executive, legislative, judicial and Tribal Council branches. A useful direct source for the structure of the contemporary Oklahoma government.

sources.title: History of the Northern Arapaho Tribe
sources.publisher: The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder
sources.annotation: Historical synthesis covering Plains homelands, northern and southern trajectories, Wind River settlement and assimilation policies. Undated language-speaker estimates and older assessments of contemporary life are not treated as current measurements.

sources.title: Language
sources.publisher: The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder
sources.annotation: Introduces Algonquian affiliation and distinctive Arapaho linguistic development, with links to lessons, grammar, stories and dictionaries. Its undated speaker counts are not used as present-day statistics.

sources.title: Stories: Sand Creek Massacre
sources.annotation: Describes the 1864 attack and descendant-led oral histories that helped locate the massacre site before its opening in 2007. Shows how family knowledge contributed to historical research.

relationshipNote: Northern Arapaho Tribe and the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes are separate governments. Cheyenne people are distinct from Arapaho people despite alliance and a shared Oklahoma government; Wind River is shared with the distinct Eastern Shoshone people.

name: Arikara
overview: Arikara, also known as Sahnish or Sáhniš, are a distinct Indigenous people of the Missouri River region. They are one of the three peoples of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation at Fort Berthold. Farming villages, regional trade, displacement and sustained language work connect their history with contemporary community life.

sections.title: Sahnish identity within a shared nation
sections.text: Sahnish is the people’s own name, while Arikara appears widely in historical English-language records. Arikara belongs to the Caddoan language family, distinct from the languages of Mandan and Hidatsa neighbors. The contemporary Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation, also called the Three Affiliated Tribes, brings these three peoples into one government on the Fort Berthold Reservation in North Dakota. Similar houses and shared political institutions should therefore not be mistaken for a single original language or an undifferentiated tribal identity.

sections.title: Agriculture, earthlodges and exchange
sections.text: Arikara villages combined substantial earth-covered houses with gardens on Missouri River bottomlands. Women grew corn, beans and squash, built lodges and processed food and hides. Hunting, wild plants and preserved foods complemented agriculture. These communities were also important participants in intertribal exchange; the National Park Service describes Arikara traders as intermediaries in regional networks. Their history challenges the idea that Plains peoples shared one uniformly mobile, bison-dependent economy. Village life involved skilled construction, cultivation, storage and exchange as well as seasonal hunting.

sections.title: Epidemics, movement and the three-peoples alliance
sections.text: Successive smallpox epidemics and pressure from warfare forced changes in the location and organization of Arikara villages. North Dakota Studies describes severe epidemics in 1837 and 1856. MHA Nation’s history records Sahnish settlement at Star Village and subsequent movement into Like-a-Fishhook Village in the early 1860s following attacks on Star Village and Fort Berthold. Mandan and Hidatsa people had established Like-a-Fishhook earlier. Their alliance and proximity grew through shared needs for security while each people retained its own history.

sections.title: Garrison Dam and the loss of river communities
sections.text: MHA Nation’s history explains how Garrison Dam displaced people from fertile Missouri bottomlands to less productive uplands. Elbowoods and neighboring communities were dismantled or submerged, affecting homes, gardens, cemeteries and local relationships. The Nation dates completion of relocation to fall 1954, with the agency moving to New Town. It emphasizes that replacement infrastructure did not restore the old village communities: families became scattered, and some agricultural livelihoods could not be rebuilt. This was a profound transformation of social life as well as land use.

sections.title: Language work and accessible learning materials
sections.text: MHA Nation’s language department presents Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara separately and identifies all three as central to community identity. Its resource library brings together learning books, children’s materials, stories, recordings and other teaching resources. An Arikara section links past class recordings and handouts, while the site recognizes the work of Elders, teachers, Nueta Hidatsa Sahnish College and the MHA Language Project. These materials support active learning and intergenerational transmission. Language endangerment should not be used as a claim that Arikara people or culture have disappeared.

sections.title: Government and living interpretation
sections.text: The MHA Nation’s Tribal Business Council includes a chair and representatives from six geographic segments, linking governance to communities across the reservation. Its public services include education, health and housing institutions. The Nation also manages a reconstructed Earthlodge Village near New Town, where interpreters share the histories and cultures of the three peoples. Reconstruction is a present-day educational undertaking, rather than an untouched nineteenth-century village. It creates another way for the public to encounter community knowledge while recognizing the people who continue to govern and interpret their own history.

sources.title: Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation
sources.annotation: Official government entry point explaining the Three Affiliated Tribes, Fort Berthold location, six segments, Tribal Business Council and services. Population figures and individual officeholders are intentionally omitted from the profile.

sources.title: MHA Nation History: Villages, Relocations and Land Loss
sources.annotation: Nation-published timeline of distinct village histories, the alliance at Like-a-Fishhook and Garrison Dam relocation. Especially valuable for the community account of losses that monetary compensation and new infrastructure did not repair. The page gives conflicting 1862/1863 dates for the Like-a-Fishhook move; the profile uses the early 1860s.

sources.title: Language
sources.annotation: Current Nation portal for the three languages, downloadable materials and Arikara class recordings. Recognizes specific community teaching projects and warns that older language websites and applications are being updated.

sources.title: Section 1: Arikaras
sources.publisher: North Dakota Studies / State Historical Society of North Dakota
sources.annotation: Educational account of Sahnish naming, villages, agriculture, kinship and epidemics, illustrated with archival photographs. Exact Like-a-Fishhook arrival dates vary across and within the historical accounts; this profile uses the early 1860s.

sources.title: Arikara
sources.publisher: National Park Service / Gateway Arch National Park
sources.annotation: Synthesis of Caddoan affiliation, farming villages and trade, followed by Lewis and Clark journal excerpts. The excerpts contain colonial prejudice; this profile uses the introduction rather than treating explorers’ judgments as neutral descriptions.

sources.title: Mandan Hidatsa Arikara Tourism Earth Lodge Village
sources.annotation: Identifies the reconstructed Earthlodge Village as managed by MHA Nation and describes its educational interpretation. It concerns all three peoples and should not be treated as an exclusively Arikara village.

relationshipNote: Arikara/Sahnish is a distinct people within MHA Nation. Mandan and Hidatsa are allied constituent peoples, not aliases for Arikara. Fort Berthold is the reservation and governmental setting, rather than the whole historical homeland.

name: Assiniboine
overview: Assiniboine is an outside name for northern Plains peoples who use names including Nakoda, Nakota and Nakona in community contexts. Their histories and kinship cross the Canada–United States border, while contemporary governments remain distinct. Fort Belknap, Fort Peck and Saskatchewan First Nations offer different perspectives on land, language and continuing political life.

sections.title: Names, language and origin accounts
sections.text: Fort Belknap’s history identifies Assiniboine people as Nakoda or Nakota. Assiniboine derives from an Ojibwe name associated with cooking with heated stones. These names should be read in their local contexts. Linguistically, Nakoda belongs to the Siouan family. Linda Cumberland’s grammar also cautions against an old classification that treated Nakoda simply as a minor variant of Dakota and Lakota. Linguistic relationships do not settle every question of historical origin: Fort Belknap preserves oral accounts that differ from familiar outsider migration narratives.

sections.title: Bison, mobility and trade networks
sections.text: Bison supplied food, hides and materials for mobile Plains communities. Assiniboine people also traded meat and pelts with Missouri River agricultural communities for crops and other goods. Their relations with European trading companies built on Indigenous knowledge, diplomacy and exchange. At Fort Union, founded in 1828, Assiniboine permission enabled the post’s establishment, and Assiniboine traders became its principal partners. Women’s marriages and kinship relationships helped sustain those connections. This history places Indigenous communities at the center of the trading economy rather than at its margins.

sections.title: Epidemics and the coercion of reservation life
sections.text: Smallpox repeatedly devastated northern Plains communities, including Assiniboine people connected with the Upper Missouri trade. The University of Saskatchewan’s synthesis places these epidemics alongside changing commercial networks and the destruction of bison herds. It describes later reserve life as shaped by restricted mobility, hunger, residential schooling and prohibitions on cultural and political activities. These pressures differed across the international boundary and among local communities. Reservation settlement consequently cannot be explained as a simple voluntary abandonment of older lifeways or as the end of Indigenous collective identity.

sections.title: Carry the Kettle and Cypress Hills homelands
sections.text: FHQ Developments’ community account dates the Treaty 4 adhesion by ancestors of Carry the Kettle to September 25, 1877 at Fort Walsh. It identifies the western Cypress Hills, including the Head of the Mountain, as a homeland of enduring significance. The community-authored history Owóknage follows forced removal from those lands to the area south of Sintaluta, Saskatchewan. Its published contents bring together land use, treaty-era farming, language, sacred places, harvesting and environmental concerns, drawing on Elder interviews as well as documentary research.

sections.title: Distinct peoples within contemporary governments
sections.text: Fort Belknap Indian Community in Montana unites Nakoda and Aaniiih, also called Gros Ventre, in a shared government. The reservation was established in 1888 and represents only part of the peoples’ wider ancestral territories. Fort Peck institutions separately serve Assiniboine and Sioux communities; their language department distinguishes Nakona/Nakoda from Dakota. Carry the Kettle is another particular First Nation rather than a name for all Assiniboine people in Canada. Shared institutions, broad peoplehood and individual governments therefore need to be kept distinct when tracing contemporary sovereignty.

sections.title: Language renewal and community knowledge
sections.text: Fort Peck’s language department describes revitalization through community curriculum, Elder stories, history, songs and daily cultural learning. Its stated vision includes developing immersion education, which should be distinguished from evidence that a particular new school has already opened. Cumberland’s 2025 grammar provides a complementary reference on Nakoda sounds, grammar, kinship and writing systems, with attention to different practical orthographies. Community teaching and scholarly documentation serve related purposes, but the authority of particular speakers, families and institutions remains essential to how knowledge is learned and shared.

sources.title: Fort Belknap History
sources.annotation: Community account of Nakoda and Aaniiih, reservation history, bison lifeways and oral histories. Contains differing origin narratives and older linguistic simplifications; this profile preserves that distinction and uses a recent grammar for classification.

sources.title: The Assiniboine
sources.publisher: National Park Service / Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site
sources.annotation: Specific account of Assiniboine authority and partnerships at Fort Union, intertribal exchange and the 1837 epidemic. Older broad origin claims and exact demographic estimates are not adopted here.

sources.title: Carry the Kettle
sources.annotation: First Nations economic organization’s community history of the 1877 Treaty 4 adhesion and Cypress Hills homeland. The page’s legal-case update is explicitly historical and is not used as a current litigation status.

sources.title: Owóknage: The Story of Carry The Kettle Nakoda First Nation
sources.publisher: Carry the Kettle First Nation / University of Regina Press
sources.annotation: Publisher-distributor description and detailed contents of a community-authored history arising from traditional land-use research. Provides a substantial reading route through Cypress Hills displacement, Elder testimony, harvesting and sacred places; full book access is separate.

sources.title: Fort Peck Tribes Departments: Language & Culture
sources.annotation: Official department page states the Nakona/Nakoda and Dakota program’s mission and vision for curriculum and immersion education. Distinguish its goals from confirmation that every envisioned facility is operational.

sources.title: A Grammar of Nakoda (Assiniboine), Linda A. Cumberland (2025)
sources.annotation: Public description, contents and chapter introductions establish Siouan affiliation, critique older classification and describe grammatical and orthographic coverage. Full text requires library or other access; this profile uses publicly visible material.

sources.title: The Nakota/Nakoda Oyadebi (Assiniboine)
sources.publisher: Gladue Rights Research Database / University of Saskatchewan
sources.annotation: Historical synthesis of cross-border territory, trading alliances, epidemics and coercive reserve policies. Includes community and further-reading links; used for context rather than as a substitute for each nation’s own history.

relationshipNote: Assiniboine/Nakoda is not one government. Aaniiih/Gros Ventre at Fort Belknap and Dakota at Fort Peck are distinct co-resident peoples. Stoney Nakoda has close historical and linguistic relationships, but a Nakoda spelling alone does not identify the same community, language variety or government.

name: Atakapa
overview: The Atakapa-Ishak are Indigenous people of the Louisiana–Texas Gulf Coast whose descendants maintain organized communities and cultural work. Ishak is a self-designation; Atakapa is an outside name. Language documentation now supports renewed learning, while community histories challenge older publications that confused reduced visibility in colonial records with disappearance.

sections.title: Names, homelands and community scope
sections.text: Ishak approximately means people or human beings. Atakapa derives from a Choctaw expression translated as man-eater; the Nation's account challenges its use as evidence of cannibalism and explains its dehumanizing colonial history. Traditional homelands extend from Vermilion Bay in Louisiana toward Galveston Bay in Texas. The name therefore connects several local histories, rather than denoting a single settlement or an organization representing every descendant.

sections.title: Coastal life and colonial encounters
sections.text: Historical accounts describe mobile bands fishing, hunting and gathering within familiar coastal and bayou territories. Alligators supplied meat, oil and hides. French trade and Spanish mission projects drew different groups into colonial networks: the Deadoses had a brief association with San Ildefonso, one of the San Xavier missions abandoned in 1755. The Handbook distinguishes Atakapas east of the lower Neches from associated groups farther west. Its dated demographic framing should not be used as a census of living descendants.

sections.title: A wider Afro-Indigenous context
sections.text: Louisiana Creole Peoplehood places Indigenous erasure and anti-Blackness together within histories of land, kinship and cultural continuity. Its editors bring community interviews, autobiographical writing and scholarship into an account of Afro-Indigenous agency, including foodways, language revitalization and diaspora. This broader scholarship supplies context for the Nation's description of interwoven Ishak and Creole histories. It does not establish that every Louisiana Creole belongs to an Ishak organization, or that different communities share one political membership.

sections.title: Ishakkoy documentation and renewed learning
sections.text: Ishakkoy, also called Yukhíti Koy, is classified as a language isolate. The Living Dictionary adapts David Kaufman's 2022 dictionary, prepared with Ishak community collaborators from earlier Gatschet and Swanton materials. Its data were moved online in 2024–2025. The resource includes words, example sentences and grammatical explanation, making an older documentary corpus more usable. The digitized 1932 Bureau of American Ethnology dictionary provides a complementary historical record whose transcription practices and outsider interpretations must be distinguished from contemporary community choices.

sections.title: Living organizations and cultural expression
sections.text: The Nation of Southwest Louisiana identifies several organized Ishak groups, including the Attakapas Opelousas Prairie Tribe and Grand Bayou Indian Village. It also describes new poetry, songs and narratives in Ishakkoy. These are examples of continuing cultural authorship. Shared heritage should not erase organizational differences or turn interrupted language transmission into a measure of whether the people exist.

sources.title: Our Story
sources.annotation: Community account explaining Ishak naming, Gulf Coast homelands, distinct organized groups and contemporary writing in Ishakkoy. Especially valuable for correcting disappearance narratives in older reference works.

sources.title: Atakapa Indians
sources.annotation: Dorothy Couser's historical overview supplies coastal subsistence, trade and mission context. Its dated assertions about cannibalism and demographic disappearance should be assessed against living Ishak accounts.

sources.title: Louisiana Creole Peoplehood: Afro-Indigeneity and Community
sources.publisher: University of Washington Press / Rain Prud'homme-Cranford, Darryl Barthé and Andrew J. Jolivétte, editors
sources.annotation: Publisher's description of the 2022 community-and-scholar anthology provides broader Afro-Indigenous context. The book itself requires borrowing or purchase; its overview cannot establish individual tribal membership.

sources.title: Atakapa Ishākkoy Living Dictionary
sources.publisher: Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages / David V. Kaufman and Ishak collaborators
sources.annotation: Searchable collaborative dictionary with a project history, grammar overview and examples. Explains the relationship between Kaufman's revised dictionary and the earlier Gatschet–Swanton documentation.

sources.title: A Dictionary of the Atakapa Language: Accompanied by Text Material
sources.publisher: Bureau of American Ethnology; digitized by University of North Texas Libraries
sources.annotation: Full digitized 1932 Gatschet–Swanton dictionary, with page images and text navigation. A primary documentary resource, best read with the contemporary Living Dictionary and community interpretation.

relationshipNote: Atakapa is a historical outside label; Ishak is a self-designation. The people and their associated historical groups are broader than any single present-day Ishak organization.

name: Atikamekw
overview: The Atikamekw Nehirowisiw are a distinct nation whose homeland, Nitaskinan, lies in the interior of Québec. Manawan, Opitciwan and Wemotaci have their own councils and cooperate through Atikamekw Sipi. Language, family responsibilities for territory and the assertion of continuing sovereignty connect community life with wider political and environmental concerns.

sections.title: Nitaskinan and territorial responsibility
sections.text: Manawan's account locates identity in a territory inhabited by ancestors and entrusted to future generations. It describes a family system in which responsibility for managing a territory passes between generations; collective belonging differs from individual land ownership. Rivers, travel routes and place names connect Manawan with the Saint-Maurice, Outaouais and neighboring watersheds. This understanding of homeland reaches beyond the boundaries of any one reserve and beyond Québec's more recent administrative regions.

sections.title: Language and knowledge
sections.text: Nehirowimowin is the Atikamekw language. Manawan's language page presents speech, territory and identity as inseparable, emphasizing vocabulary shaped by local environments and the self-designation Nehirowisiw. It also describes relationships with other Algonquian-speaking peoples, without making those nations interchangeable. Québec's profile identifies Atikamekw-language educational materials among Atikamekw Sipi's services. The combination matters: language is both an everyday medium of community life and a means through which institutions transmit knowledge and support younger generations.

sections.title: Industrial development and displacement
sections.text: Québec's historical summary places a major turning point in early twentieth-century industrial forestry. A sawmill at La Tuque and the railway's expansion toward Wemotaci and Abitibi brought workers and other resource users into Atikamekw territories. Dam building caused further moves between 1950 and 1972. These developments changed access to land and patterns of settlement. They should be understood as interventions in an existing homeland, rather than as the beginning of Atikamekw history or presence in the region.

sections.title: Local councils and nation-wide cooperation
sections.text: Atikamekw Sipi, founded in 1982, works across Manawan, Opitciwan and Wemotaci. Its published governance structure distinguishes ordinary members, elected representatives with voting responsibilities and the board made up of the Grand Chief/President and the three community chiefs. The assembly uses consensus, while the board uses majority decisions. Social, educational, linguistic and technical services operate alongside political representation and negotiations. These overlapping institutions show why the nation, its coordinating council and its three local governments should be identified separately.

sections.title: The 2014 sovereignty declaration
sections.text: On September 8, 2014, the nation's leaders publicly affirmed continuing sovereignty over Nitaskinan. Their declaration states that the territory had not been ceded or sold and links governance to occupation, language, inherited responsibilities and relationships with neighboring nations. It demands Atikamekw consent for resource development and use. This is the nation's political position and statement of rights; it should not be confused with a completed territorial settlement or a declaration that Canadian and Québec authorities have accepted every claimed jurisdiction.

sources.title: Territoire
sources.annotation: Manawan's explanation of collective territorial belonging, intergenerational management responsibilities, travel routes and local place names. Its perspective is specifically grounded in Manawan.

sources.title: Langue
sources.annotation: Community explanation connecting Nehirowisiw identity, language and environmental knowledge. Provides a first-person complement to external linguistic classifications.

sources.title: Atikamekw
sources.annotation: Provincial profile updated May 9, 2025, summarizing the three communities, industrial forestry, dam-related moves and Atikamekw Sipi's services. Its undated population estimate is not repeated here.

sources.title: Gouvernance
sources.publisher: Atikamekw Sipi – Conseil de la Nation Atikamekw
sources.annotation: The council's account of assembly membership, board composition, voting rules and administrative responsibilities. Search-indexed full text was inspectable although direct retrieval intermittently failed.

sources.title: La nation Atikamekw-Nehirowisiw dépose une déclaration de souveraineté !
sources.annotation: Indigenous publisher's August 14, 2015 account reproduces the leaders' September 8, 2014 declaration. Read the declaration as an Atikamekw assertion, separately from the article's broader legal commentary.

relationshipNote: Atikamekw Nehirowisiw names the nation. Manawan, Opitciwan and Wemotaci are distinct communities with local governments; Atikamekw Sipi coordinates representation and services across them.

name: Atsugewi
overview: Atsugewi homelands lie south of the Pit River in northeastern California, including Hat Creek and Dixie Valley. Atsugewi identity has both local historical dimensions and a place within the present Pit River Tribe. Language archives, seasonal land-use histories and the work of Atsugewi cultural interpreters provide complementary routes into that continuing history.

sections.title: Homelands and seasonal movement
sections.text: Hat Creek connected fishing grounds, winter settlements and routes into the Lassen highlands. In warmer months, Atsugewi people traveled along Hat Creek and Lost Creek into areas now within Lassen Volcanic National Park. Snow and elevation shaped seasonal use rather than making the high country uninhabited or without owners. National Park Service interpretation distinguishes the Atsuge of the pine-covered Hat Creek area from the Apwaruge of the drier country farther east; Berkeley also identifies Dixie Valley within the language's traditional area.

sections.title: Atsugewi within the Pit River Tribe
sections.text: The Pit River Tribe's own introduction identifies eleven autonomous bands, including Atsugewi, whose homeland encompasses parts of Shasta, Siskiyou, Modoc and Lassen counties. Atsugewi is consequently neither a synonym for every Pit River person nor simply an obsolete label. The modern tribal framework brings distinct bands together while acknowledging their autonomy. Readers should also distinguish Ajumawi, a band name in the Tribe's list, from the spellings Achumawi or Achomawi used in linguistic and historical publications.

sections.title: Language relationships and the documentary record
sections.text: Berkeley's California Language Archive identifies Atsugewi and Achumawi together as Palaihnihan, while describing the larger Hokan grouping as a hypothesis. Linguistic relatedness does not make the languages identical. The archive's guide points to D. L. Olmsted's 1984 lexicon and Leonard Talmy's 1972 dissertation, Semantic Structures in English and Atsugewi, alongside archival collections. These resources preserve vocabulary and analysis, but each reflects particular speakers, collection circumstances and scholarly questions rather than an exhaustive account of Atsugewi knowledge.

sections.title: Women as public cultural educators
sections.text: Selena LaMarr began interpreting Atsugewi cultural practices at Lassen in June 1952 and became the park's first woman naturalist. She demonstrated basket weaving and acorn processing outside the Loomis Museum, wearing Atsugewi dress as her park uniform. Dessie Snooks joined the work in 1954; Laverna Jenkins and Lillian Snooks later continued demonstrations. Their teaching documents named Atsugewi people's active roles in deciding what visitors learned, rather than treating baskets and food-processing tools as anonymous remains of the past.

sections.title: Continuity and the limits of archival categories
sections.text: Park accounts describe tribal participation in identifying museum collections and reviewing exhibits and publications. The Tribe's own website also advertises Pit River language sessions, although that announcement alone does not establish their Atsugewi-specific content. Berkeley's statement about the absence of first-language Atsugewi speakers draws on a 2011 linguistic reference. It describes language transmission at that source's date, not the disappearance of a people, the end of learning, or the authority of outsiders to define present Atsugewi belonging.

sources.title: American Indian Heritage
sources.publisher: Lassen Volcanic National Park, National Park Service
sources.annotation: Park overview describes Hat Creek seasonal travel, Atsuge and Apwaruge regional distinctions, and tribal collaboration on collections and interpretation. Relevant Atsugewi passages are separated from the page's other peoples.

sources.title: Atsugewi
sources.publisher: California Language Archive, University of California, Berkeley
sources.annotation: Specialist guide to the language area, proposed relationships, archival collections, Olmsted's lexicon and Talmy's dissertation. Speaker-status wording cites Golla 2011 and should retain that temporal context.

sources.title: Official Home of the Pit River Tribe
sources.annotation: Tribal government's own identification of eleven autonomous bands and their regional homeland. The authoritative starting point for the contemporary political relationship; includes language-program announcements.

sources.title: Selena LaMarr
sources.annotation: Biographical account details LaMarr's 1952–1972 interpretive work and the participation of Dessie Snooks, Laverna Jenkins and Lillian Snooks. Offers named cultural teachers alongside generalized ethnographic descriptions.

relationshipNote: Atsugewi is distinct from Achumawi, although the languages are related and the peoples share Pit River connections. Atsugewi is also one of the Pit River Tribe's eleven autonomous bands.

name: Awaswas
overview: Awaswas names an Ohlone language associated with the north shore of Monterey Bay and the Santa Cruz region. Its speakers belonged to distinct local communities, including the Uypi. Descendant histories continue through the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band, whose cultural and land-stewardship work connects this regional history with living people and present responsibilities.

sections.title: A language region with distinct local peoples
sections.text: Awaswas is useful as a linguistic and regional label, but it should not turn every historical community into a single centralized tribe. The Santa Cruz Museum identifies its own site as Uypi homeland and describes the Uypi as Awaswas-speaking. The Amah Mutsun Tribal Band explains that its ancestors belonged to numerous communities with distinct territories and leadership, linked through trade and marriage. Ohlone supplies a broader connection, while Awaswas, Uypi and Amah Mutsun identify different aspects of that history.

sections.title: Missionization and descendant continuity
sections.text: Spanish missions brought people from different villages under coercive institutions that disrupted family life, land access, ceremonies and language use. The Amah Mutsun Tribal Band traces its lineages to communities affected by Mission Santa Cruz and Mission San Juan Bautista. Its history describes forced relocation, restrictions on leaving the missions and the continuation of practices under repression. The present Band is therefore a descendant community shaped by this history, rather than a convenient substitute for supposedly vanished people.

sections.title: What survives in the linguistic record
sections.text: The California Language Archive locates Awaswas on Monterey Bay's north shore and identifies it as one of the Ohlone languages, distinct from Mutsun, Rumsen and others. Its documentation survives in wordlists rather than a large recorded speech corpus. The guide links published Pinart and Henshaw vocabularies and William Shipley's study of Awaswas. Such limited material supports research into vocabulary and relationships, but cannot be treated as a complete dictionary of community knowledge or as evidence that descendants ceased to exist.

sections.title: Returning to stewardship
sections.text: The Amah Mutsun Land Trust states that its purpose includes conserving cultural and natural resources in the territories of both Mutsun- and Awaswas-speaking peoples. It describes a 2005 Tribal Council decision to renew stewardship, the creation of the Trust in 2013 and incorporation in 2015. Partnerships with landowners restore access for ceremony, learning and land care. Its stated area extends from Año Nuevo through the Santa Cruz Mountains and Monterey Bay to the Pajaro, San Benito and Salinas watersheds.

sections.title: Environmental pressures are cultural concerns
sections.text: California's climate-impact account describes drought, wildfire, changing rainfall and rising seas as threats to Amah Mutsun physical, spiritual and cultural health. Culturally important plants become harder to restore, while erosion exposes and destroys coastal archaeological places. The account highlights the cumulative effects of fire suppression, land management and climate change in the 2020 CZU fires. These concerns connect historical Awaswas territories to contemporary stewardship; they should not be reduced to museum preservation or separated from the people responsible for those places.

sources.title: First Peoples of California
sources.publisher: Santa Cruz Museum of Natural History
sources.annotation: Local exhibit identifies Uypi homeland and Awaswas language, explains food processing and material practices, and states that displayed local materials involve Amah Mutsun consultation. Useful for geographically specific learning.

sources.title: Land Trust: Our Mutsun Identity
sources.annotation: Tribal account explains the distinct territories and leadership of ancestral communities and the contemporary Band's shared identity. The page links onward to the Land Trust's newer website.

sources.title: History
sources.annotation: The Band's extended account of mission coercion, suppressed practices and continuing family lineages. Contains some inconsistent dates and older recognition-process statements; those details are not adopted in this profile.

sources.title: Awaswas
sources.publisher: California Language Archive, University of California, Berkeley
sources.annotation: Specialist overview identifies the language's area, Ohlone relationships and wordlist-based documentation. Provides specific Pinart, Henshaw and Shipley references rather than a generic language search.

sources.title: Our History and Vision
sources.annotation: The Trust's own account dates its stewardship initiative and organizational development and explicitly includes Awaswas-speaking territories. Distinguishes conservation activity from claims about historical political boundaries.

sources.title: Impacts of climate change on the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band
sources.publisher: California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment
sources.annotation: August 2023 summary links climate hazards, culturally important species, coastal sites and tribal stewardship. Its environmental discussion connects descendant community priorities with the broader Awaswas–Mutsun region.

relationshipNote: Awaswas is a historical Ohlone language and regional label; Uypi names a local Awaswas-speaking people. The Amah Mutsun Tribal Band includes descendants of Awaswas- and Mutsun-speaking communities. These terms are related but not interchangeable.

name: Awakateko
overview: Awakateko people have their principal homeland around Aguacatán in Huehuetenango, Guatemala, with communities also established in Mexico. Their Maya language is called Qa'yool or Qyool in Mexican sources. Community-led language research, school materials and migration histories reveal an identity rooted in a particular highland region while extending across national borders.

sections.title: Names and a highland homeland
sections.text: Mexico's Indigenous-peoples atlas records qatanum, meaning our people, as a self-designation and explains Awakateko through the place name Aguacatán. The community's own linguistic atlas locates its homeland at the foot of the Sierra de los Cuchumatanes. Awakateko is one of several distinct Maya languages, rather than another word for Maya as a whole. Its close linguistic relationship with Ixil should also be distinguished from the similarly spelled Akateko, a different language and people in this directory.

sections.title: Displacement and communities in Mexico
sections.text: INALI connects the Awakateko presence in Mexico with flight from Guatemala's civil war and military repression. Its migration account describes the relocation of Guatemalan Indigenous communities to different Mexican states in 1984–1985, followed by further movement for work, including to the United States. A newer INALI profile specifically identifies Maya Tecún I, Maya Tecún II and Santo Domingo Kesté in Champotón, Campeche. These settlements belong to a transnational history; migration does not make Aguacatán the only legitimate location of Awakateko life.

sections.title: Work, clothing and adaptation
sections.text: The INPI ethnography describes garlic and onion cultivation, seasonal crops, sheep raising, weaving, professional employment and agricultural migration. Its discussion of women's clothing identifies embroidered huipiles, woven skirts and sashes as forms of cultural expression. These are examples within a changing community, not a dress requirement or a complete occupational portrait. The same account notes adaptation of plant knowledge after settlement in Chiapas and Campeche, where different climates and vegetation created new conditions for everyday life.

sections.title: Hearing local variation directly
sections.text: The Atlas Lingüístico Sonoro del Awakateko is led by the Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka within Guatemala's Maya-language academy, with advice from CIESAS and CIMSUR-UNAM. Its first version compares 400 entries from nine Aguacatán communities through maps, recordings and practical and phonetic transcriptions. Two speakers represent each location. Differences occur in sounds, word forms and vocabulary, sometimes within one community. This direct evidence shows why INALI's single catalogued Mexican variety should not be read as proof that everyone speaks identically.

sections.title: Teaching and community authorship
sections.text: In June 2025, Guatemala's government news agency reported the distribution of approximately 2,050 copies of Literatura Maya: Principios y Valores Culturales Awakateko to schools in Aguacatán. The Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka coordinated with educational authorities, reaching institutions at several school levels. Alongside its sound atlas and earlier grammars, this work places community knowledge into learning materials. It also changes the research perspective: Awakateko speakers are authors, investigators and teachers, rather than merely subjects counted in endangered-language statistics.

sources.title: Awakatecos – Etnografía
sources.publisher: Instituto Nacional de los Pueblos Indígenas
sources.annotation: Ethnographic overview provides qatanum self-designation, work, dress and adaptation in Mexican settlements. Treat its generalized cultural descriptions as examples, rather than universal practices; full indexed text was inspected.

sources.title: Atlas Lingüístico Sonoro del Awakateko (ALISA)
sources.publisher: Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka / Academia de las Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala, with CIESAS and CIMSUR-UNAM
sources.annotation: Community-led interactive atlas with 400 entries, nine research locations, speaker recordings and transparent sampling methods. Explains local variation and provides a bibliography of community grammars and dictionaries.

sources.title: Lengua Qa'yool (awakateko)
sources.annotation: Binational overview identifies Aguacatán and named Campeche settlements and describes the Awakateko–Ixil relationship. Its Mexican catalog classification is administrative in scope; demographic totals are not used here.

sources.title: Atlas de las Lenguas Indígenas de México: Awakateko
sources.annotation: Detailed migration discussion connects civil-war displacement, 1984–1985 relocations and later labor mobility. Other panels use older census data, so their present-tense wording should be dated carefully.

sources.title: ALMG impulsa idioma awakateko con distribución de documento en centros educativos
sources.annotation: June 16, 2025 report documents a specific Awakateko-led school-material distribution, naming participating institutions and the publication. Provides a dated example of language work beyond endangerment summaries.

relationshipNote: Awakateko is a particular Maya people and language, closely related linguistically to Ixil. It is distinct from Akateko despite the similar spelling. The ALMG linguistic community is a language institution, not a government over every Awakateko community.

name: Ayapaneco
overview: Ayapaneco refers to a language and community associated with Ayapa in Jalpa de Méndez, Tabasco. Also called Ayapa Zoque or numde 'oode, the language belongs to the Mixe-Zoque family. Community authors, teachers and media projects provide a fuller introduction than sensational stories about a disappearing language and its supposedly last speakers.

sections.title: Ayapa and the language's names
sections.text: Ayapa lies on Tabasco's Gulf coastal plain, near the Cuxcuxapa River, in a region shaped by cacao cultivation and contact among Zoque, Nahua, Chontal and other populations. Ayapaneco is also called zoque-ayapaneco or Ayapa Zoque; numde 'oode, numdi oode and numte oote appear in different publications. These spellings refer to the language, not separate peoples. Linguist Jhonnatan Rangel places it in the Mixe-Zoque family and treats interrupted transmission as a specific linguistic challenge.

sections.title: Community life beyond speaker counts
sections.text: INPI's account describes a community with agricultural work, trades, shops, professional employment and migration to regional cities. Cacao remains part of foodways through drinks such as pozol and chorote. Patron-saint celebrations create occasions for local and neighboring communities to gather, with San Miguel especially significant. These practices connect livelihood, food and collective identity. They also show why the number of fluent speakers cannot stand in for the number of community members or the extent of their cultural life.

sections.title: Reading work by named community authors
sections.text: Las partes del cuerpo humano en ayapaneco was published in 2013 under the authorship of Manuel Segovia and José Manuel Segovia, with other Ayapaneco speakers credited as collaborators. It combines an introduction, discussion of sounds and writing, illustrated vocabulary and a glossary in Ayapaneco, Spanish and English. The introduction explicitly notes that spelling was not standardized at publication. This makes the book both a practical learning resource and evidence of community authorship, while warning against treating its orthography as timeless or universally fixed.

sections.title: Public teaching and language celebration
sections.text: INALI's report of the first Ayapaneco language festival in May 2013 describes workshops with schoolchildren, poetry, theater, music and traditional games in Ayapa. Materials about the body and a collection of legends were prepared with speakers and distributed during the event. The report recognizes several named contributors, including Manuel Segovia, Isidro Velásquez and Cirilo Velásquez. This dated account documents collaborative teaching and public recognition; it does not establish the size or results of any program in 2026.

sections.title: Ayapanet and access to recorded knowledge
sections.text: A contribution by Rangel with the independent community collective Retoño de mis Raíces describes documentation and revitalization work since 2012. Their Ayapanet project responds to a practical problem: audiovisual materials existed, but local infrastructure made them difficult to use. They proposed a low-cost media library accessible through a local wireless network without internet. The contribution describes a testing phase, not a completed universal service. Its emphasis is community control over content and access, alongside education and language learning.

sections.title: Understanding endangerment without the media shortcut
sections.text: Daniel Suslak's 2011 article examines the circulation and consequences of the story that Ayapaneco was dying because two speakers refused to talk to one another. Its abstract traces publicity through institutions and international media. That anecdote cannot replace the documented work of multiple contributors. Rangel's research identifies limited documentation, costly annotation, scarce equipment and unreliable connectivity as obstacles, and links language work with inequality and discrimination. These structural conditions give a more useful context for understanding revitalization needs.

sources.title: Ayapanecos – Etnografía
sources.publisher: Instituto Nacional de los Pueblos Indígenas
sources.annotation: Detailed account of Ayapa's coastal setting, work, cacao drinks and patron-saint celebrations. Full indexed text was inspected; its speculative language-origin claim is excluded from this profile.

sources.title: Challenges for Language Technologies in Ayapaneco
sources.publisher: Jhonnatan Rangel / Language Technologies for All
sources.annotation: Research poster identifies Mixe-Zoque affiliation and practical barriers involving annotation, equipment, connectivity and training. Its speaker estimates describe the research context and are not repeated as present-day totals.

sources.title: Las partes del cuerpo humano en ayapaneco
sources.publisher: Manuel Segovia and José Manuel Segovia / Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas
sources.annotation: 2013 illustrated book by named community authors, crediting additional speakers. Includes sound and spelling guidance, body vocabulary and a trilingual glossary; explicitly states that its spelling was not standardized.

sources.title: Primer festival de la lengua ayapaneca: Shem yeh chotz numdi oode
sources.annotation: May 13, 2013 release records children's workshops, locally compiled publications and named speakers honored at the festival. The site's migrated title contains 2025, but the actual event and release are from 2013.

sources.title: Ayapanet: creando una mediateca virtual comunitaria soberana, in Experiencias en educación popular y tecnologías libres
sources.publisher: Jhonnatan Rangel with Retoño de mis Raíces / Universidad Popular
sources.annotation: Pages 49–50 describe a community collective's local media-library project and its testing stage. Offers a collaborative first-hand account of documentation access and control, rather than an outsider rescue narrative.

sources.title: Ayapan Echoes: Linguistic Persistence and Loss in Tabasco, Mexico
sources.annotation: 2011 study analyzes the circulation and consequences of the two-speakers story. The freely readable abstract and bibliography were inspected; full article access may require a subscription.

relationshipNote: Ayapaneco names a language and associated community in Ayapa; it is a particular member of the Mixe-Zoque family. Language transmission, community membership and the broader Zoque label are related but separate matters.
