name: Babine
region: British Columbia / Babine Lake and Babine River
overview: Babine histories connect lake and river communities, salmon fisheries, hereditary leadership, and relationships across north-central British Columbia. This introduction centers Lake Babine Nation’s own publications, alongside collaborative scholarship and public records. Its reading collection follows historical trade and colonial interference through language learning, community planning, stewardship, and work toward self-government.

sections.title: A nation of connected communities
sections.text: Lake Babine Nation’s community plan organizes its discussion around Tachet, Fort Babine or Wit’at, Old Fort, Pinkut Lake/Donald’s Landing, and Woyenne, alongside members living away from home. This is a network of communities with shared and distinct priorities, rather than one village whose location captures the entire homeland. The treaty office’s public account places the traditional territory around Babine Lake and describes four clans and hereditary leaders with responsibilities toward land. Its institutional and treaty-stage descriptions are older material, however, and should not be taken as a current administrative directory.

sections.title: Balhats and the study of law
sections.text: The balhats, or feast system, belongs within an account of law, leadership, and responsibilities. In Cis dideen kat—When the Plumes Rise, Jo-Anne Fiske and Betty Patrick frame their study as a descriptive account of Lake Babine customary law and changing relations with the Canadian state. Their publicly available introductory chapter explains that research began in 1993 and that historical documents were examined alongside the knowledge of hereditary chiefs and elders. They explicitly acknowledge limits concerning narratives, territorial detail, and language. Their work offers an important sustained reading path without making one study a complete or timeless statement of Lake Babine law.

sections.title: Trade, salmon, and historical records
sections.text: The treaty office reproduces Daniel Williams Harmon’s account of his January 1812 journey among Babine villages. It describes hospitality, salmon-based livelihoods, and trade connections reaching toward the coast through neighboring peoples. The office also warns that Harmon’s knowledge was limited by observation and interpretation. His writing is a record of a colonial visitor encountering an already connected society. It does not mark the beginning of Babine history, establish an exact population, or supply an objective description of every community. Reading the excerpt with the office’s commentary makes the source’s position visible.

sections.title: The barricade dispute and community resistance
sections.text: In its account of 1906, the treaty office describes women defending a rebuilt fishing weir when fisheries officers attempted to dismantle it. It recounts arrests and negotiations in which chiefs sought provisions and services in exchange for removal of the weirs. The account calls the resulting agreement the Barricade Treaty. This history connects colonial control of fishing to food security, resistance, and political negotiation. A later UNBC report describes archaeological work conducted with Lake Babine Nation at a Babine River fishing village, where earlier work had established occupation extending back at least 1,300 years. The collaborative study concerns a particular site, not a date for the origins of the people.

sections.title: Language learning and public resources
sections.text: Nedut’en is the name used by Lake Babine Nation’s FirstVoices collection. Its public pages offer an alphabet, recordings, words, phrases, and stories; individual records identify contributors. These are community-created learning resources, with their own access and reuse conditions. FPCC’s March 2025 account adds a specific example of intergenerational learning: Brian Lacerte learning from his mother, Rosalie MacDonald, through a mentor-apprentice program. It also describes MacDonald’s own learning and teaching work. Together, the collection and dated account show different forms of language transmission. Neither provides grounds for a current speaker census or a claim that one teaching method represents every family.

sections.title: Planning, governance, and the Foundation Agreement
sections.text: The 2017–2022 community plan records priorities in language, education, housing, access, health, and stewardship, developed through engagement with members. It is evidence of community priorities during a stated planning period; it is not a report that all goals were achieved. The Nation’s November 2020 update explains the Foundation Agreement as a twenty-year framework for implementing rights and developing self-government, rather than a finalized treaty settlement. Its governance page describes a proposed Nation-level and community-level model and steps toward ratification and implementation. A February 2024 federal announcement records a further funding agreement supporting governance capacity and infrastructure priorities for Wit’at and Tachet. That announcement documents commitments, not the completion of all funded facilities or a transition to the proposed government.

sections.title: Stewardship and decisions about development
sections.text: Lake Babine Nation’s environmental-assessment explanation identifies sustainability, benefits, socioeconomic effects, and respectful relationships as criteria for evaluating proposed development. It distinguishes an assessment collaboration agreement from work toward a further consent agreement. A different publication, issued in July 2023, announced closure of the recreational salmon fishery along part of the Babine River corridor in response to warm water and pressure on salmon. Read as a dated action, it shows how stewardship is expressed through decisions concerning food, water, and future generations. The notice should not be used as current fishing guidance. More recent regulations and Nation communications would need checking before a visit.

sources.title: Who We Are
sources.annotation: Community account of territory, four clans, hereditary responsibilities, and the treaty office’s mandate. Its older treaty-stage and membership statements are not used as current facts.
sources.reviewScope: Identity and mandate paragraphs; the page contains dated administrative context.

sources.title: Comprehensive Community Plan 2017–2022
sources.annotation: Nation-authored plan built through member engagement. See printed pp. 7–10, 20–26 and the community chapters for scope, shared priorities, and local differences. Goals are not completion reports.
sources.reviewScope: Introduction, community structure, shared directions, and operational priorities; not every implementation action was independently checked.

sources.title: Cis dideen kat—When the Plumes Rise: introductory chapter
sources.publisher: Jo-Anne Fiske and Betty Patrick · UBC Press
sources.annotation: Public sample of the coauthored book on Lake Babine legal order. The introduction, printed pp. 7–14, explains its research, historical context, and explicit limits. The entire book has not been reviewed here.
sources.reviewScope: Publisher’s eight-page introductory sample; the full book is a further reading option.

sources.title: Daniel Williams Harmon Visits Babine Lake, January 1812
sources.annotation: Community commentary plus a reproduced fur-trader journal excerpt, useful for early trade and salmon livelihoods. The publisher identifies the visitor’s limited perspective; his estimates are not treated as a census.
sources.reviewScope: Commentary and reproduced January 1812 journal passage.

sources.title: The Barricades Are Protected and the Treaty Is Made, 1906
sources.annotation: Nation-published narrative of women’s defense of the weir, arrests, and negotiations. Distinguish this historical account from the legal text and later interpretation of the Barricade Treaty.
sources.reviewScope: Full historical narrative; no claim that every treaty obligation or its legal status has been independently established.

sources.title: Excavation Uncovers Centuries-worth of Artifacts for Northern BC First Nation
sources.annotation: October 18, 2012 account of archaeology undertaken with Lake Babine Nation, including earlier dating of a fishing-village site. A project report about one location, not a complete regional archaeological synthesis.
sources.reviewScope: Full project news account; later technical publications remain a research task.

sources.title: Nedut’en (Lake Babine Nation): public language collection
sources.annotation: Community-created alphabet, dictionary, recordings, and stories. Public pages and a dictionary example were inspected; follow contributor credits and the collection’s usage conditions. Counts and audio transcriptions are not reproduced here.
sources.reviewScope: Rendered public home/alphabet/collection and sample dictionary material; no restricted content accessed.

sources.title: National Indigenous Languages Day: Nedut’en mentor-apprentice account
sources.publisher: First Peoples’ Cultural Council, with Odette Auger
sources.annotation: March 31, 2025 feature includes Brian Lacerte and Rosalie MacDonald’s Lake Babine learning and teaching experiences. Its other language-community examples are not assigned to Lake Babine.
sources.reviewScope: Nedut’en section, including the named mentor-apprentice pair and teaching account.

sources.title: Foundation Agreement Update — November 2020
sources.annotation: Nation-published explanation of the September 2020 agreement and implementation work. See printed pp. 3 and 10–11, especially the distinction between a framework agreement and a treaty settlement.
sources.reviewScope: Introductory account, timeline, and questions and answers; goals and early commitments kept distinct from later outcomes.

sources.title: Governance: Foundation Agreement vision and milestones
sources.annotation: Sets out a proposed two-level governance model, community engagement, citizenship-rule development, ratification, and implementation steps. Its future-tense model is not described as already in force.
sources.reviewScope: Governance vision and milestone sections; no current officeholder list used.

sources.title: Environmental Assessment and the Foundation Agreement
sources.annotation: Explains the Nation’s criteria for proposed development and distinguishes collaboration from a further consent agreement. A public account of priorities, not a substitute for the signed instruments.
sources.reviewScope: Assessment criteria, collaboration/consent distinction, and policy explanation.

sources.title: Lake Babine Nation Closes Recreational Fishery
sources.annotation: July 28, 2023 announcement of protective action effective August 1, 2023, linking river temperature and pressure on salmon. Historical evidence of stewardship; not current fishing guidance.
sources.reviewScope: Full public announcement and its stated 2023 effective date.

sources.title: Governance capacity and Wit’at/Tachet infrastructure funding agreement
sources.publisher: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada
sources.annotation: February 21, 2024 announcement, with a Lake Babine leadership statement, of support for capacity and community priorities. Funding commitments do not establish that every project or governance transition was completed.
sources.reviewScope: News-release body and Lake Babine statement; demographic and reserve-count figures omitted.

relationshipNote: This profile centers Lake Babine Nation and its communities. Language labels such as Babine, Nedut’en, and Babine–Witsuwit’en require context; linguistic relationships do not make Lake Babine, Wet’suwet’en, or Dakelh governments interchangeable. The historical Barricade Treaty and the 2020 Foundation Agreement are different instruments.
researchGaps: Read the full Fiske–Patrick volume and subsequent community scholarship; compare accounts of women’s leadership, law, colonial violence, relocation, and residential schooling.

Follow the Barricade Treaty account into the original instrument, archival correspondence, and community interpretations of unfulfilled obligations. Compare the community plan’s 1905 chronology with the treaty office’s 1906 narrative.
Add more histories authored by individual communities and clarify the wider scope of historical Babine and related language labels.
Check newer community reports for the outcomes of governance, infrastructure, environmental-assessment, and language initiatives. Source quantity does not establish completion.

name: Bannock
overview: Bannock histories connect the Snake River Plain with Northern Paiute communities and wider Great Basin and Rocky Mountain travel networks. At Fort Hall, Bannock and Shoshone people share the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes government while maintaining distinct languages. Community publications connect treaty history, language teaching, food sovereignty, and environmental stewardship.

sections.title: People, language relationships, and homelands
sections.text: Bannock is both a people’s name and the name of a Northern Paiute language variety. Linguist Tim Thornes locates historical Bannock territory around the Snake River Plain of southwestern Idaho and the Boise River Valley, and describes sustained contact with Shoshoni. The Tribes’ own overview places Bannock bands within a shared history with Northern Shoshone bands, across ancestral lands extending well beyond present reservation boundaries. Their related Numic languages belong to the Uto-Aztecan family. A shared government and close cultural relationships coexist with linguistic distinctions; neither Bannock nor Northern Paiute should be treated as simply another name for Shoshone.

sections.title: Routes, place names, and responsibilities to land
sections.text: The Language and Cultural Preservation Department’s 2024 essay describes Tennambo’i, the lava-flow country now within Craters of the Moon, through ancestral memory and living place names. It connects routes across the Snake River Plain with salmon fishing, buffalo hunting, and camas and wild-carrot gathering farther afield. These paths linked important food areas and relationships across a large region. The department also explains its work with the National Park Service to bring tribal interpretations into public signage. Its account connects historical travel with present responsibilities, including collaborative efforts against invasive grass threatening camas habitat at Centennial Marsh.

sections.title: The treaty, an unfulfilled reservation promise, and Fort Hall
sections.text: The treaty signed at Fort Bridger on July 3, 1868, contains different provisions for Eastern Shoshone and Bannock people. Article 2 promises a future Bannock reservation; the published text names Portneuf and “Kansas Prairie,” while the Tribes’ public interpretation identifies Camas Prairie. Article 4 addresses reservation residence and hunting on specified unoccupied lands. In its Treaty Day account, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes explains that the separate Bannock reservation was never created and that Bannock people were instead relocated to Fort Hall in 1869. The Tribes’ historical overview describes subsequent losses through surveying, legislation, and allotment. Reading the treaty beside tribal interpretation helps distinguish the agreement’s text from what the United States actually implemented.

sections.title: Camas, colonial deprivation, and food sovereignty
sections.text: A 2023 study coauthored by tribal citizens and university researchers connects the Bannock War of 1878 with restricted access to food, damage to camas grounds, and unmet federal obligations. Its historical discussion places hunger and displacement at the center of the conflict rather than describing war as an isolated outbreak. The study also documents a contemporary project to make camas more accessible at Fort Hall through cultivation experiments and community activities. Seeds and transplanted bulbs offered possible ways to strengthen access, although the authors identify questions about genetic differences and longer-term effects. This work connects experimental science, tribal oversight, and relationships maintained through food.

sections.title: Language teaching and a narrator’s history
sections.text: The Tribes’ Language and Cultural Preservation Department describes instruction in both Bannock and Shoshone, taught by tribal members and connected to history, identity, and treaty knowledge. Its archival and digital preservation programs retain documents, recordings, interviews, and family histories. Thornes’s 2020 publication provides a different kind of evidence: Bannock-language narratives with transcription, grammatical analysis, and translation. The autobiographical narrative of Lizzie Edmo was recorded by Sven Liljeblad at Fort Hall in 1959. Her recollections describe travel, gathering, fishing, and exchanges among families. The article preserves an individual speaker’s experience and linguistic knowledge; it should not be generalized into a single life story for every Bannock family.

sections.title: Shared government and the care of public history
sections.text: The published constitution and bylaws identify the Fort Hall Business Council as the governing body of the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes and provide for seven elected members. The document records a constitution approved in 1936 and later amendments. This is a primary source for the shared government’s formal structure, rather than a description of every earlier Bannock political arrangement. Cultural work is also institutional: the preservation department maintains archives, supports historical research, and addresses misleading representations and exploitation of tribal intellectual property. Its museum presents community history, art, and the Benedicte Wrensted photographic collection. Publicly shared information sits alongside material the department explicitly treats as confidential or sensitive.

sections.title: Horses and knowledge passed within families
sections.text: The Tribes describe Indian relay racing as a continuing horse tradition passed to younger generations by tribal families. Its public explanation outlines a team of four people and three horses, with the rider changing horses between laps while teammates manage the exchanges. This gives readers a concrete view of coordination and skill. The page’s broader claims about the sport’s origin represent the Tribes’ own account; this profile does not turn its undated historical claims into a precise chronology.

sections.title: Fish, water, energy, and contemporary priorities
sections.text: The shared government’s Fish and Wildlife Department links habitat restoration and fisheries work to the exercise of treaty rights. The Tribes’ salmon advocacy also calls for removal of the four lower Snake River dams, framing recovery as a cultural responsibility as well as an ecological issue. Its Water Resources Department describes protection of water quality, administration of reservation water use, and implementation of the 1990 Fort Hall water agreement. A separate 2022 Community Action Plan brings air monitoring, community survey findings, renewable energy, and efficiency measures into environmental planning. Together these sources show distinct forms of contemporary tribal action. They document governmental priorities and proposals, rather than proving that every proposed project or policy has been completed.

sources.title: About: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes — culture and history
sources.annotation: Tribal historical overview, especially “Culture and History” and the reservation discussion. Explains the shared community’s composition, food resources, travel, and land reduction. Undated; its broad regional account is not a map of exclusively Bannock territory.

sources.title: Bannock (Fort Hall, Idaho)
sources.publisher: International Journal of American Linguistics / University of Chicago Press
sources.annotation: Tim Thornes, 2020, volume 86 supplement 1, pp. S13–S33. Read the introduction, Lizzie Edmo’s autobiographical narrative, and recording notes. Specialist linguistic analysis accompanies older speaker recordings; the article’s speaker estimate is dated, not a current census.
sources.author: Tim Thornes

sources.title: Embracing Tennambo’i: The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes’ Connection to Craters of the Moon
sources.publisher: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes Language and Cultural Preservation Department / National Park Service
sources.annotation: Tribal department’s guest essay, updated September 25, 2024. Explains place names, ancestral travel, interpretive collaboration, and camas habitat restoration. This is an explicitly tribal-authored perspective hosted by the park, not an anonymous federal summary.

sources.title: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, 1868
sources.publisher: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes, reproducing Charles J. Kappler’s treaty compilation
sources.annotation: Primary treaty text dated July 3, 1868; inspect Articles 2 and 4 for the promised Bannock reservation and hunting provision. Published in Kappler’s 1904 compilation and reproduced by the Tribes. Historical wording requires context and does not by itself settle present legal disputes.

sources.title: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes recognize Fort Bridger Treaty Day
sources.annotation: Public tribal interpretation of the treaty, its continuing importance, the unfulfilled separate Bannock reservation, and relocation to Fort Hall. Complements the primary text by explaining the government’s own historical and political understanding. No publication date is displayed in the inspected article.

sources.title: Strengthening Relationships to Traditional Foodways: Adapting Food Practices Through Camas Cultivation Experiments on the Fort Hall Indian Reservation
sources.annotation: Sidney Fellows, Georgia Hart-Fredeluces, Nolan Brown, and Morey Burnham, 2023. Tribal–university collaboration; read “Postcolonial Suppression,” partnership methods, and conclusions. Connects restricted food access and 1878 conflict to cultivation research, while identifying biological uncertainties. Historical discussion is a synthesis, not a complete war history.
sources.author: Sidney Fellows; Georgia Hart-Fredeluces; Nolan Brown; Morey Burnham

sources.title: Language and Cultural Preservation
sources.annotation: Substantive departmental account of instruction, archives, historical research, oral-history recording, museum work, and protection of sensitive knowledge. Undated; class times, personnel, and visitor details require a fresh check before use. Programs serve the shared Shoshone-Bannock community.

sources.title: Constitution and Bylaws for the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes
sources.annotation: Constitution approved April 30, 1936, presented with amendments through August 15, 2013. Read the preamble and governing-body provisions for the seven-member Business Council. The web transcription repeats an article heading incorrectly; consult the linked official document for precise legal citation.

sources.title: Indian Relay Racing
sources.annotation: Community account of family horse traditions, relay-team roles, and changing horses during a race. Useful for the Tribes’ own public presentation of the sport. Undated origin and age claims are attributed accounts, not an independently established chronology.

sources.title: Fish and Wildlife: preserving resources and Snake River policy
sources.annotation: Departmental explanation of treaty-based responsibilities, restoration priorities, and salmon and steelhead projects. Read “Management Authority,” “Areas of Focus,” and “Snake River Policy.” Broad program descriptions are undated; announcements and project implementation dates need separate verification.

sources.title: Save Idaho Salmon
sources.annotation: Tribal advocacy page explains cultural stakes of salmon recovery, the Snake River policy, and support for lower Snake River dam removal. Includes named community perspectives and discussion of a 2021 congressional proposal. Read as a policy position, not proof of a completed dam-removal decision.

sources.title: Tribal Water Resources Department and Commission
sources.annotation: Tribal account of the 1990 Fort Hall water agreement, department formation, water-use administration, and quality monitoring. Read “History and Direction” and “Water Quality Program.” Explains governmental responsibilities; it is not a substitute for the agreement’s full legal text.

sources.title: Community Action Plan: Promoting Cleaner Air Through the Development of Renewable Energy Resources
sources.publisher: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes, Tribal Department of Energy
sources.annotation: Dated November 15, 2022. Read printed pp. 1–4 for purpose, pp. 10–14 for community survey, pp. 15–21 for monitoring, and pp. 29–31 for implementation. A planning document with community input; recommended actions and dated measurements are not current outcome evaluations.

relationshipNote: Bannock is closely connected to Northern Paiute and shares government with Shoshone people at Fort Hall. Bannock and Shoshoni are linguistically distinct. Sources about the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes describe shared institutions and should not be presented as evidence of a separate contemporary Bannock-only government.
researchGaps: Add more Bannock-authored or community-approved family histories and public oral histories, including experiences beyond Fort Hall; one narrator cannot represent every band or family.
Deepen the 1878 war account with community interpretation and critically assessed archival records, including differing experiences among Bannock, Northern Paiute, and Shoshone families.

Compare the published treaty text with manuscript and official publication records, and document the chronology of Fort Hall boundary changes without collapsing promises, executive orders, and later legislation into one event.
Add a dated community account of Bannock language learning and teaching outcomes; no current speaker total is asserted here.
Expand evidence on schooling, livelihoods, art, and family life, and verify permissions and cultural suitability before reproducing archival images or knowledge.

name: Beothuk
overview: Beothuk histories belong to Newfoundland’s coasts, islands, rivers, and interior. Archaeology, the testimony and drawings of named Beothuk women, and Mi’kmaw perspectives reveal skilled communities responding to colonial pressures. Their histories also require separating the destruction of communities from claims about ancestry, language, and the authority to tell their story.

sections.title: Names, homelands, and the archaeological record
sections.text: The name Beothuk appears in vocabularies recorded from Demasduit and Shanawdithit, although European writers used several spellings. Archaeologists commonly connect historically documented Beothuk with the island’s earlier Little Passage complex. These are analytical labels: they do not make every ancient Newfoundland site Beothuk. Donald Holly shows how older scholars mixed materials from different periods and peoples, then used the resulting collections to portray Beothuk as an isolated survival from a remote past. A more careful history distinguishes particular sites, dates, and communities while recognizing connections across the surrounding region.

sections.title: Seasonal places and food knowledge
sections.text: Beothuk communities combined coastal and inland resources, with movements shaped by local opportunities rather than one island-wide timetable. Seals, salmon, seabirds, shellfish, caribou, and plant foods contributed to their livelihoods. At Boyd’s Cove in Notre Dame Bay, shell deposits helped preserve animal bones that Newfoundland’s acidic soils often destroy. These remains document a varied diet alongside house pits and other occupation evidence. Coastal and river access therefore mattered together: describing Beothuk simply as interior caribou hunters would mistake a later situation of displacement for the full range of their land use.

sections.title: Making, travel, and adaptation
sections.text: Birchbark canoes supported travel on inland waterways and at sea. Surviving models, drawings, and written descriptions preserve evidence about their distinctive construction, although no full-sized Beothuk canoe survives. At Boyd’s Cove, nails and other European metal were reshaped into projectile points, scrapers, awls, and ornaments. Acquiring material from fishing stations could provide useful iron without sustained participation in a European fur trade. Laurie McLean’s comparison of house pits further argues that settlement and architecture changed differently across places and periods. These findings show selective innovation and changing decisions, not an unchanging culture.

sections.title: Contact, dispossession, and responsibility
sections.text: Colonial violence, competition for shorelines and food, and disease transformed Beothuk lives. Yet early contact should not be reconstructed by projecting later violence backward without evidence. William Gilbert’s reassessment finds that fragmentary sixteenth-century documents do not support a simple history of permanent hostility from first contact. Qalipu First Nation’s community plan also challenges the mercenary myth that blamed Mi’kmaq for Beothuk destruction and portrayed Mi’kmaq as outsiders brought to Newfoundland by the French. This matters because historical storytelling has affected living Indigenous peoples’ identities and claims to their homeland.

sections.title: Beothuk women as historical authorities
sections.text: Oubee, Demasduit, and Shanawdithit supplied much of the surviving recorded vocabulary, under circumstances shaped by capture and coercion. Shanawdithit’s drawings document homes, foods, family relationships, travel, killings, and encounters with settlers. Her work offers a Beothuk account within an archive largely assembled and annotated by outsiders. Sarah Roberts’s 2024 study follows her capture in 1823, years in the Peyton household, transfer to St. John’s, and death in 1829. The Rooms reported revising the colonial descriptions attached to her drawings in 2023–24, showing that even catalogue labels carry interpretations requiring scrutiny.

sections.title: Language and the limits of documentation
sections.text: The principal written word lists came from Oubee, Demasduit, and Shanawdithit through different recorders. Linguist John Hewson brought these materials together into a master list of 325 glosses, with numerals and month names. Their survival is significant, but the evidence is limited and filtered through inconsistent transcription. Scholars have disagreed about whether, and how closely, Beothuk belongs with Algonquian languages. The language guide summarizes both Hewson’s argument for a relationship and Ives Goddard’s skepticism. It is therefore preferable to present the affiliation as debated rather than confidently equating Beothuk with Innu-aimun or Mi’kmawi’simk.

sections.title: Survival narratives, ancestry, and DNA
sections.text: Shanawdithit is often called the last Beothuk, but Mi’kmaw oral histories challenge the conclusion that nobody survived beyond her death. Historical community destruction, genealogical descent, genetic relationships, and present political identity are different questions. Duggan and colleagues’ 2017 ancient-DNA study distinguishes sampled Maritime Archaic and Beothuk maternal populations. Carr’s 2020 comparison finds some ancient maternal lineages identical or close to modern ones, while emphasizing sampling limits and warning against simplistic genetic identity assignments. Mitochondrial DNA follows one maternal line; it cannot by itself confirm or exclude all Beothuk ancestry, establish an unbroken genealogy, or decide community membership.

sections.title: Repatriation and continuing responsibilities
sections.text: In March 2020, the remains of Demasduit and Nonosabasut returned from Scotland to Newfoundland and Labrador after advocacy led by Miawpukek Saqamaw Mi’sel Joe and cooperation among Indigenous leaders, museums, and governments. The provincial announcement records Indigenous leaders’ own statements about ancestors, responsibility, and the harm of colonial collecting. The Rooms’ 2024–25 report documents the Final Resting Place Circle’s continuing deliberations and a request for support to return associated spiritual belongings held in Britain. Those are dated reports of work in progress, not evidence that every repatriation or burial question has since been settled.

sources.title: Comprehensive Community Plan — Early History of Mi’kmaq in Ktaqmkuk
sources.annotation: Read the historical discussion around printed pages 17–18. This community-owned plan traces the unsupported mercenary story through colonial writers and explains its continuing consequences for Newfoundland Mi’kmaq. It supplies a living First Nation’s perspective, not a claim to speak for all Beothuk descendants.

sources.title: Shanawdithit — Provincial Historic Commemorations research paper
sources.author: Sarah Roberts
sources.annotation: Five-page study with reproduced drawings and source references. Pages 1–4 describe Shanawdithit’s knowledge, family, capture, testimony, death, and commemoration; the opening explicitly acknowledges Mi’kmaw challenges to the last-Beothuk narrative. Historical descriptions are retained with a language advisory.

sources.title: Beothuk Language
sources.author: Ingeborg Marshall
sources.publisher: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage Website, Memorial University
sources.annotation: Explains the three surviving vocabularies, their archival transmission, and disagreement about Algonquian affiliation. Identifies recorders and circumstances of collection; its classification should not be treated as settled consensus.

sources.title: Precontact Beothuk Land Use
sources.publisher: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage Website, Memorial University
sources.annotation: Detailed account of coastal and inland food resources, preservation, seasonal movement, and local variation. Sections on evidence explicitly distinguish archaeological findings from possibilities. The page now flags its 2009 scholarship as requiring updating; this profile uses it for documented resource relationships rather than speculative population totals.

sources.title: The Boyd’s Cove Beothuk Site
sources.author: Ralph T. Pastore
sources.publisher: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage Website, Memorial University
sources.annotation: The excavator explains site discovery, preservation of food remains, house pits, and iron refashioning; see Beothuk Diet and Reasons for Avoiding the Fur Trade. Its broader conclusions about extinction and other peoples reflect an older interpretive framework, explicitly flagged by the website, and require comparison with newer Indigenous perspectives.

sources.title: Transportation
sources.author: Ingeborg Marshall
sources.publisher: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage Website / Beothuk Institute
sources.annotation: Specialist account of canoe forms, bark construction, surviving models, snowshoes, and winter transport, based on Marshall’s historical research. It distinguishes observed objects and descriptions from reconstruction and inference. No surviving full-sized canoe is available to resolve every construction detail.

sources.title: Beothuk Housepits: Barometers of Historic Transition
sources.author: Laurie McLean
sources.annotation: Archaeological synthesis comparing 22 coastal and 64 Exploits Valley house pits; see pp. 1–9 and 42–44. Differences in architecture and artifacts support varied responses to colonial pressures. Interpretations of household organization and motives remain archaeological arguments, not direct testimony from every community.

sources.title: Beothuk-European Contact in the 16th Century: A Re-evaluation of the Documentary Evidence
sources.author: William Gilbert
sources.annotation: Peer-reviewed reassessment, pp. 24–44, of early captives, voyages, geographical names, and possible trade. Paragraphs 40–44 distinguish what fragmentary documents establish from assumptions repeated by later writers. Its challenge to perpetual early hostility does not deny well-documented later colonial violence.

sources.title: A Historiography of an Ahistoricity: On the Beothuk Indians
sources.author: Donald H. Holly Jr.
sources.annotation: Author-uploaded full text of the peer-reviewed article, DOI 10.1080/0275720032000107383. Pages 129–136 examine mixed artifact collections and assumptions about isolation, language, and inevitable disappearance. Valuable for reading older scholarship critically; its own discussion predates subsequent ancient-DNA work and current Indigenous-led debates.

sources.title: Genetic Discontinuity between the Maritime Archaic and Beothuk Populations in Newfoundland, Canada
sources.author: Ana T. Duggan and colleagues
sources.annotation: Full open-access research article, DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2017.08.053. Results and Figure 3 analyze ancient maternal genomes alongside archaeological and isotope evidence. The study concerns sampled maternal populations and explicitly allows possible ancestry in living people; it is not a test of present community identity or every line of descent.

sources.title: Evidence for the persistence of ancient Beothuk and Maritime Archaic mitochondrial DNA genome lineages among modern Native American peoples
sources.author: Steven M. Carr
sources.publisher: Genome 63, pp. 349–355; author copy at Memorial University
sources.annotation: Read Discussion and Assignment of individuals, pp. 352–354. Compares ancient maternal lineages with modern database sequences, explains limited sampling and the Santu Toney inheritance example, and cautions against simplistic commercial ancestry claims. Miawpukek cooperation and approval are acknowledged. The afterword supersedes an earlier withdrawn manuscript.

sources.title: Nonosabasut and Demasduit Returned to Newfoundland and Labrador
sources.publisher: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, with statements by Indigenous leaders
sources.annotation: Primary announcement of the transfer into The Rooms’ care, with attributed statements from Mi’sel Joe and other Indigenous leaders. Its backgrounder uses a categorical extinction account and describes the administrative recognition position in 2020; those passages should not settle contested historical or contemporary identity questions.

sources.title: The Rooms Annual Report 2023–2024 — revising Beothuk collection descriptions
sources.publisher: The Rooms Corporation, Newfoundland and Labrador
sources.annotation: Printed pp. 76–77 (PDF pages 38–39) document the Final Resting Place Circle’s initial meeting and revision of colonial labels for Shanawdithit’s drawings and Demasduit portraits. This institutional self-report explains present cataloguing responsibilities and the influence of Cormack and Howley’s assumptions on collections.

sources.title: The Rooms Annual Report 2024–2025 — Final Resting Place Circle
sources.publisher: The Rooms Corporation, Newfoundland and Labrador
sources.annotation: Printed p. 66 (PDF page 69) describes the Circle’s June 2024 visits, deliberations about a resting place, and request for support to repatriate spiritual belongings held in Britain. This is a dated progress account; it does not establish a final burial decision or the outcome of later requests.

relationshipNote: Beothuk, Innu, and Mi’kmaq remain distinct directory entries. Regional connections, oral histories, and shared or related maternal lineages do not make these names interchangeable. This profile does not adjudicate living people’s membership or ancestry claims.
researchGaps: Add fuller Indigenous-authored oral-history material and inspect Chief Mi’sel Joe’s published interview and Santu Toney scholarship directly; neither is counted merely because other works cite it.
Obtain a specialist linguistic assessment of recent classification arguments and inspect original word-list manuscripts alongside their later transcriptions.
Verify developments after the 2024–25 museum reporting year concerning final resting places and spiritual belongings; do not infer completion from earlier announcements.
Extend site-specific archaeological coverage beyond northeast Newfoundland and keep competing interpretations of continuity, social organization, and colonial violence explicitly attributed.

name: Biloxi
overview: Biloxi histories connect the Mississippi Gulf Coast with communities in Louisiana, Texas, and beyond. Biloxi is a Siouan language, distinct from Tunica. Biloxi descendants participate in the contemporary Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, whose shared government and cultural work preserve several ancestral identities rather than a single interchangeable tribal past.

sections.title: Names, identity, and a shared nation
sections.text: A public family heritage website established in 2003 by Donna Pierite, Elisabeth-Michele Pierite, and relatives records the self-designation Taneks Hanyadi and several European spellings of Biloxi. Variant names are useful when searching archives, but those records must be interpreted in context. The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe describes its citizens as carrying Tunica, Biloxi, Ofo, Avoyel, and Choctaw heritages, with people identifying as Tunica, Biloxi, or Biloxi-Choctaw. These continuing identifications sit within a shared political community. They should not be flattened into a claim that Tunica and Biloxi originally spoke the same language or had identical histories.

sections.title: The Gulf Coast and movements into Louisiana
sections.text: The tribe’s historical account places Biloxi people in the Pascagoula River region when French expeditions encountered them in 1699. Earlier routes are less securely documented. Linguist David Kaufman has proposed southern Appalachian connections using language and place-name evidence, while acknowledging unresolved identifications. His linguistic argument is a hypothesis about an earlier past, not a dated map of an established homeland. The federal acknowledgment dossier likewise cautions that later movements involved several locations and extended periods. It discusses Biloxi communities near the Mississippi, Coulee des Grues, and Bayou Boeuf, rather than describing everyone as making one simultaneous migration west.

sections.title: Texas: alliance, expulsion, and diplomacy
sections.text: Megan Biesele’s historical overview traces Biloxi families along the Neches River in East Texas by 1828. It situates their subsequent movements within European settlement pressures and the Republic of Texas’s campaigns against Cherokee and allied communities in 1839. The same account follows other Biloxi groups through later Texas settlements and relationships with neighboring peoples. The 1843 Bird’s Fort treaty provides a complementary primary record: its proclamation names the Biloxi among the participating nations, and its signature page identifies a Biloxi chief as Hoyo Tubby. Together, these sources document negotiation as well as displacement; they do not establish the later affiliation of every Biloxi family.

sections.title: Community connections and federal acknowledgment
sections.text: The 1980 acknowledgment dossier distinguishes the Marksville community from a closely connected Biloxi-Choctaw community at Indian Creek in Rapides Parish. It describes kinship and continuing association, while recognizing uncertainty about earlier settlements. The tribe’s own history records Biloxi authorization in October 1924 for Eli Barbry to pursue union with the Tunica. Federal recognition followed in 1981, after generations of community efforts. The dossier is valuable evidence of that administrative process, not an authority that created the people’s existence. Contemporary self-government also includes a tribal court; its own program description discusses civil cases, housing, estates, and interpretation of tribal governing documents.

sections.title: Reading the Biloxi language record critically
sections.text: Biloxi belongs to the Southeastern, also called Ohio Valley, branch of Siouan and is closely related to Ofo and Tutelo. Dorsey and Swanton’s 1912 dictionary preserves Biloxi vocabulary, phrases, and thirty-one texts. Swanton’s introduction explains that he reorganized Dorsey’s unfinished materials and changed transcription conventions. The published record therefore contains both speakers’ contributions and editorial decisions. Kaufman’s later reanalysis argues that an incomplete exchange of two vowel symbols during editing makes mechanical conversion into a modern spelling unreliable. His study compares cognates and other records to reassess individual words. These works preserve substantial linguistic knowledge, while leaving uncertainties that readers should retain rather than silently resolve.

sections.title: Language relationships and the art of speaking
sections.text: Language scholarship also reveals Biloxi participation in a multilingual region. Kaufman’s 2016 comparison examines shared vocabulary and grammatical patterns involving Biloxi, Ofo, and other Lower Mississippi Valley languages. He distinguishes similarities inherited from Siouan ancestry from those potentially arising through contact; the direction of particular borrowings often remains uncertain. A separate study of Biloxi narrative particles considers how speakers expressed differing degrees of certainty about possible events. Such analyses go beyond lists of translated words to questions of storytelling and interpretation. They are scholarly readings of a limited historical corpus, and should not be mistaken for a description of every Biloxi speaker’s practice.

sections.title: Living cultural work, plants, and public institutions
sections.text: The Tunica-Biloxi Language and Culture Revitalization Program connects language classes with crafts, stories, songs, and youth activities. Its published language curriculum concerns Tunica. A 2026 article coauthored by tribal members and collaborators makes that distinction explicit while describing a wider community effort to reconnect ethnobotanical knowledge, basketry materials, and land stewardship. Elisabeth Pierite recounts learning basket traditions through family visits and regional gatherings; the authors discuss restoration and access to plant resources alongside an evolving guidebook. These are accounts of adaptation and continuity in the present. The tribe’s Cultural and Educational Resources Center brings an exhibit hall, preservation laboratory, and research library together on the reservation, providing a community-based route for further study.

sources.title: General Profile: The Tunica-Biloxi Indians of Louisiana
sources.annotation: The tribe’s substantial historical account covers Biloxi Gulf Coast connections, the 1924 union, recognition, and contemporary institutions. Much of the earlier narrative concerns Tunica history. Its proposed identification of a sixteenth-century Biloxi ruler is interpretive rather than settled evidence; no undated population figures are used.

sources.title: Taneks Hanyadi: What about the Biloxi language?
sources.publisher: Pierite family heritage website, preserved by Indigifab
sources.annotation: A short, attributed community-family account established in 2003 records a Biloxi self-designation, archival name variants, and the distinction between Biloxi and Tunica. Its dated language-status statements should not be treated as a current speaker survey.

sources.title: A Dictionary of the Biloxi and Ofo Languages, Accompanied with Thirty-one Biloxi Texts and Numerous Biloxi Phrases
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology, Bulletin 47
sources.annotation: The foundational 1912 collection preserves Biloxi texts and vocabulary alongside a distinct Ofo dictionary. Reviewed the contents and Biloxi introduction, pp. 1–4, through the public-domain Wikisource transcription because the institutional PDF could not be fetched. The introduction explains editorial rearrangement and notation; this is not a full review of all texts.

sources.title: A Reanalysis of the Dorsey-Swanton U-Circumflex and U-Brève in Biloxi
sources.publisher: Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics, University of Kansas
sources.annotation: Kaufman reassesses historical vowel notation using twenty-one words, related Siouan forms, and other transcriptions. Read especially the background, data, and conclusion, PDF pp. 2–9. This is a specific philological argument, not a current account of Biloxi community size or language use.

sources.title: Biloxi Realis and Irrealis Particles
sources.publisher: Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics 32, pp. 1–7
sources.annotation: Examines two Biloxi narrative particles and how speakers may mark certainty and potential events. The discussion and conclusion distinguish analysis from unresolved questions, including proposed connections with gendered speech. It interprets archival examples rather than reporting new community fieldwork.

sources.title: Two Siouan Languages Walk into a Sprachbund
sources.publisher: Language Science Press, in Advances in the Study of Siouan Languages and Linguistics
sources.annotation: A 24-page chapter on Biloxi and Ofo participation in Lower Mississippi Valley language contact. Reviewed the introduction, distinctions between inheritance and contact, lexical comparisons, and conclusion, especially printed pp. 39–42 and 54–59. Proposed earlier Biloxi locations and borrowing directions retain explicit uncertainties.

sources.title: Recommendation and Summary of Evidence for Proposed Finding for Federal Acknowledgment of the Tunica-Biloxi Indian Tribe of Louisiana
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs; GovInfo
sources.annotation: The 1980 proposed-finding dossier includes historical and anthropological reports. Reviewed the recommendation and Biloxi sections, particularly PDF pp. 1–3, 27–28, 33, and 36–37. It distinguishes communities and states evidentiary limits. Its administrative criteria and period terminology reflect a federal recognition process, not community self-definition.

sources.title: Biloxi Indians
sources.publisher: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas
sources.annotation: Biesele’s entry follows Biloxi families, alliances, coercive movements, and diplomacy in nineteenth-century Texas. Published in 1976 and updated in 2020. Its older terminology and conjectures about earlier migration require care; it is a regional historical overview, not a present-day community description.

sources.title: Bird’s Fort Treaty Ratification Proclamation, 1843
sources.publisher: Texas State Library and Archives Commission
sources.annotation: Digitized proclamation and transcription name the Biloxi among parties to the September 29, 1843 treaty. Reviewed pp. 1–2 and the signature transcription on p. 10, identifying Hoyo Tubby. Read the complete linked document for treaty terms; the Republic’s language and diplomatic frame are historical evidence, not neutral ethnography.
authors: Republic of Texas and participating Indigenous representatives

sources.title: Language & Culture Revitalization Program
sources.annotation: The tribe explains language materials, classes, cultural workshops, youth camps, and its research library. The language teaching described is Tunica; this page does not establish a separate Biloxi language curriculum. Undated class schedules and counts are excluded from the synthesis.

sources.title: Cultural & Educational Resource Center
sources.annotation: The tribe’s own guide locates its public museum and identifies the exhibit hall, preservation laboratory, and library/research center. Useful for pursuing community-based research and understanding preservation infrastructure; the center serves the contemporary tribe and is not exclusively a Biloxi collection.

sources.title: Hɔhka Moluni: Creativity and Continuity in the Linguistic and Cultural Reclamation of Tunica-Biloxi Ethnobotany
sources.annotation: Coauthored by tribal members and academic collaborators. Reviewed the project methodology, Elisabeth Pierite’s account, restoration discussion, and footnote 1. It connects basketry and plant relationships with a developing ethnobotany guidebook; the authors explicitly identify its Indigenous-language content as Tunica. The article describes work in progress, not a finished guidebook.

sources.title: Tunica-Biloxi Tribal Court: Program Description
sources.annotation: The tribal court explains its institutional responsibilities and relationship to tribal governing documents. Used for a limited description of contemporary self-government. The undated page is a program overview, not a complete statement of current jurisdiction or legal advice.

relationshipNote: Biloxi and Tunica are distinct peoples and languages. The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe is a contemporary government with multiple ancestral communities; its Tunica language initiatives must not be relabeled Biloxi language programs. Ofo is a linguistic relative of Biloxi, while shared political history does not make these identities synonyms.
researchGaps: Add more publicly shared Biloxi family oral histories and community-authored accounts beyond the Marksville-centered collection; this profile does not map all descendants or adjudicate other communities’ identities.
Compare proposed pre-1699 Appalachian connections with additional specialist historical and archaeological scholarship. Similar names alone cannot establish a migration route or a people’s identity.

Locate and inspect the more recent Biloxi dictionaries and additional original field materials. The 2011 KU dictionary and some journal downloads were inaccessible during this review and are not counted as inspected sources.
Seek a community-authorized account of present Biloxi language learning priorities. The accessible Tunica-Biloxi language and ethnobotany materials principally document Tunica reclamation.

Thirteen inspected reading sources provide a substantial starting collection, including sources scoped to the shared Tunica-Biloxi government. This is an expanded introduction, not a completed or community-reviewed history.

sources.author: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government
sources.annotation: The Cree government's community account connects Eeyou identity, northern Québec homeland, historical Ontario lands and distinct local histories. Read the introduction, governance paragraphs and community descriptions. Scope is Eeyou Istchee, not every Cree people or language. Undated totals, officeholders and treaty-process statements are not adopted as current.

researchGaps: The old Cow Creek Umpqua publication is unrelated to Cree and should be replaced, not relabelled.
The source distinguishes local First Nations and an Eeyou regional government; these are not a single government for all Cree people.
No census counts, area totals, current officers, present treaty membership or current legal conclusions are asserted.
Keep the broader entry name Cree and kind Wider grouping / peoples. This is a limited starter reading path, not a proposed renaming of all Cree as Eeyou.
Do not add unrelated Plains Cree, Nêhiyaw or other regional assertions from this one page. No map data or canonical source was edited.

sources.contentReviewScope: Complete short article read; map citation uses opening geography and historical mound-center paragraphs. Updated August16,2024.

The full inventory may contain Indigenous historical background; that has not been checked. The full report remains unread; its relevance to Nauset people needs checking.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual NPS catalogue record and abstract read; full2025 report not inspected.

sources.title: Historic Structure Report: U.S. Coast Guard Nauset Station… — NPS DataStore
sources.annotation: Site-management background lead. Catalogue abstract concerns preservation/treatment of a1936 Coast Guard dwelling and boathouse, with a1933–1958 period of significance. This is not itself Nauset identity evidence. The full report remains unread; its relevance to Nauset people needs checking.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual NPS catalogue record and abstract read; full2008 report not inspected.

sources.title: Nauset Indians
sources.annotation: A short municipal page reproduces an older account explicitly locating Nauset people on Cape Cod in Massachusetts. Used only for historical place connection; dated population and disappearance assertions and its political subordination wording are not adopted.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete five-paragraph body inspected. Opening geography and principal-village sentence support the connection.

overview: Pensacola/Panzacola is a historical people-name associated with Pensacola Bay in West Florida. The initial reading path now points to original people-specific research and distinguishes this name from the later city and the broader archaeological Pensacola culture.

sections.title: People, city and archaeological culture
sections.text: Pensacola/Panzacola is a historical people-name associated with Pensacola Bay in West Florida. The initial reading path now points to original people-specific research and distinguishes this name from the later city and the broader archaeological Pensacola culture.

sections.title: A focused source, with limits
sections.text: DeRoche’s thesis examines documentary and archaeological evidence for the historical Panzacola. The introduction and selected pages support this initial orientation; they do not establish a positively identified excavated village. The remaining thesis, contemporary descendant connections and other original accounts need further review.

sources.title: Patrick Anthony DeRoche — In Pursuit of the Panzacola: A Historical Documentary and Archaeological Investigation
sources.publisher: University of West Florida — Patrick Anthony DeRoche
sources.annotation: DeRoche’s introduction explicitly places the historical Panzacola people around present-day Pensacola Bay in West Florida using seventeenth-century documentary accounts. His discussion distinguishes this people from the archaeological Pensacola culture; the test excavation did not establish a positive Panzacola site identification. Inspection: Actual university public download, valid-TLS HTTP 200, 2,675,875 bytes, 100 PDF pages including added cover. Cover/title; abstract printed p.viii / PDF p.9; introduction printed pp.1–3 / PDF pp.10–12; and printed p.8 / PDF p.17 were read as text/OCR. Not a complete thesis or excavation-data review. Limits: The canonical name Pensacola is retained; Panzacola is the historical people-label used by the thesis. The later city and archaeological culture are separate referents. No definitive excavated Panzacola village, coordinates, ethnicity-from-ceramics inference, contemporary recognition status or disappearance claim is adopted. This is an original student thesis with committee oversight, not a statement of consensus on every historical identification.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual university public download, valid-TLS HTTP 200, 2,675,875 bytes, 100 PDF pages including added cover. Cover/title; abstract printed p.viii / PDF p.9; introduction printed pp.1–3 / PDF pp.10–12; and printed p.8 / PDF p.17 were read as text/OCR. Not a complete thesis or excavation-data review.

researchGaps: Build a people-specific reading collection beyond the selected thesis passages; compare original documentary accounts and descendant/community histories.
The title page and repository cover differ in year. Neither a later city name nor archaeological ceramics alone establishes a people’s identity.

name: Native Hawaiian (Kānaka Maoli)
region: Hawaiian archipelago / Pacific; US-HI used as a geographic navigation region
kind: Indigenous people / language / diverse communities and institutions
overview: Begin with annotated public sources on Native Hawaiian identity, language education, land and water care, institutional roles and the 1993 federal apology. This initial source guide supports a Hawaiʻi map connection while keeping its limited coverage visible.

sections.title: An Indigenous people and a Hawaiian name
sections.text: Native Hawaiian and Kānaka Maoli identify the Indigenous people of Hawaiʻi. The university naming reference provides an attributed introduction. The 1993 resolution uses an ancestry-based definition specific to that instrument; it is not a universal enrollment rule.

sections.title: A homeland connection for the map
sections.text: The resolution connects Native Hawaiian ancestors with the islands now indexed as Hawaiʻi. This state route is a finding aid, not a parcel map or a decision on territorial rights. Island-specific histories need further research.

sections.title: The Kingdom, overthrow and a dated apology
sections.text: Congress’s 1993 resolution acknowledges United States involvement in the 1893 overthrow and apologizes to Native Hawaiians. It explicitly does not settle claims. Original Kingdom documents and Hawaiian scholarship are needed for a fuller history.

sections.title: Rebuilding everyday language education
sections.text: ʻAha Pūnana Leo traces its work to Hawaiian language educators who organized in 1983. Its account describes the first preschool at Kekaha, Kauaʻi, in 1984, followed by schools on other islands. Elders’ advice about children learning through everyday interaction shaped that work. The history also acknowledges inspiration from Māori language nests. This is a community institution’s account of rebuilding education; the page does not establish current proficiency outcomes for all Native Hawaiians.

sections.title: Learning through care for land and water
sections.text: Paepae o Heʻeia’s public collection explains how a coastal fishpond on Oʻahu uses a wall and managed water exchange to support aquatic life. Its education page describes students investigating water quality and other ecological questions while helping inform the organization’s management decisions. These accounts connect inherited environmental knowledge with contemporary learning at one place. Heʻeia’s story should not be generalized to every island, family or fishpond.

sections.title: Understanding OHA as a particular institution
sections.text: The Office of Hawaiian Affairs describes itself as a semi-autonomous state agency. Its account connects its creation with 1970s Native Hawaiian activism and the 1978 constitutional convention. It identifies advocacy, research, land management and support for community programs among its roles. Reading its own description helps distinguish a service and advocacy institution from the people as a whole. Its remit does not establish consensus on political futures or make OHA a sovereign Native Hawaiian government.

sources.title: Our History
sources.author: ʻAha Pūnana Leo
sources.annotation: Educators’ institutional account of rebuilding Hawaiian-medium education, beginning with organizing in 1983 and the first preschool in 1984. A valuable program history; historical policy claims and present outcomes still need independent comparison.
sources.documentDate: Undated live page; timeline extends through 2023
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual HTML history and timeline, lines 79–114. Photographs, linked courses, videos and private portals were not inspected.

sources.title: The Fishpond and Education — Heʻeia public learning collection
sources.author: Paepae o Heʻeia
sources.annotation: The community organization explains a coastal fishpond and connects its care with place-based ecological learning. The history and education pages are counted together as one public collection. Undated teaching schedules, output figures and ownership statements are not treated as verified current conditions.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual Fishpond body, lines 54–76; Education introduction and charter-school learning account, lines 53–61. No restricted material, oral recordings, site geometry or photographs reused.

inspectedSubresources.scope: Public introduction and charter-school learning paragraphs, lines 53–61

sources.author: Office of Hawaiian Affairs
sources.annotation: OHA describes its state-agency role, origins in 1970s activism and work supporting Native Hawaiian wellbeing. Useful for understanding this particular institution; it is not a sovereign government speaking for every Native Hawaiian perspective. Staff totals and financial claims are omitted.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual substantive About, vision, mission and overview text, lines 99–118. Linked film, program reports and current administrative rules were not reviewed.

sources.title: Public Law 103–150: acknowledgment and apology for the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi
sources.author: United States Congress
sources.publisher: United States Statutes at Large, 107 Stat. 1510–1514; Government Publishing Office / GovInfo
sources.annotation: Original 1993 federal resolution: historical recitals, apology, instrument-specific definition and non-settlement disclaimer. A dated primary instrument, not a complete history or determination of contemporary citizenship, sovereignty or remedies.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual five-page PDF text/OCR read: 107 Stat. 1510–1514, all recitals and sections 1–3. This records text inspection, not a claimed page-image transcription audit.

sources.title: Hawaiian Word of the Week: Maoli
sources.author: University of Hawaiʻi News; attributed reflection by Diamond Badajos
sources.annotation: Brief university publication identifies Kānaka Maoli as the Indigenous people of Hawaiʻi through an attributed alumna’s reflection. Included for naming and orientation only; its brevity makes it supporting material rather than a substantive research-target source.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual definition and attributed reflection, lines 34–49. Embedded video and linked dictionary were not reviewed.

relationshipNote: Native Hawaiian / Kānaka Maoli is a people-level access point, distinct from the population of the modern state and from any single agency or organization. OHA is a state agency; ʻAha Pūnana Leo and Paepae o Heʻeia are specific community institutions. The historical Kingdom, its subjects, Indigenous identity, ancestry-based program categories and contemporary political proposals require their own contexts. The state-index connection does not decide recognition, citizenship or territorial claims.
researchGaps: A fuller account needs Hawaiian-authored historical scholarship and original Kingdom-era documents, with island-specific histories.
Contemporary family voices, diaspora experiences, health and housing, and the diversity of political positions need stronger representation.
Legal program definitions, current law and recognition debates require separately dated specialist research; the 1993 resolution does not answer them all.
Learning outcomes, restoration results and present program availability have not been independently assessed.
evidenceNotes: Four substantive works/collections and one short supporting naming reference were inspected within recorded scopes on October 21, 2026. Paepae o Heʻeia pages count once. The guide is not promoted to a developed profile or an adequate initial introduction; no community review is implied.
No generated images, copied photographs, restricted cultural content or precise site coordinates were used. The 1993 law was reviewed as text/OCR, not asserted as a full image-transcription audit.
